House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. White (Leeds) for the second reading of Bill (No. 88), to provide for the appointment of a Tariff Commission and the proposed amendment of Mr. Guthrie thereto.

The objections which have been taken by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to this Bill may be summarized under three heads, first that there is no call whatever for the Bill, and no proper reason given for its introduction; second that it is a subversion of constitutional government or certainly constitutional practice in Canada and, third, that it will tend to more closely ally the question of the tariff with party politics. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), twits the Finance Minister (Mr. White, Leeds), with not having given sufficient
266b

reasons for the introduction of this Bill. It is a peculiar thing that upon very many subjects with which, on account of the very short space of time that this government have been in power, we have not yet been able to deal, we are twitted by the opposition from day to day for not introducing such legislation, or at any rate declaring our policy. Upon the debate in reply to the speech from the Throne, this House was divided, because the government had not declared its policy on the naval question. We have been twitted because we have not announced our policy with reference to the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, and we have been twitted that we have not brought down legislation with respect to the granting to the provinces the land within their borders. And yet to-day, when we do bring down legislation implementing one more of the promises made by the present Premier (Mr. Borden), when he was in opposition, we find the opposition objecting, and stating that we were not justified in enunciating our policy to the people of this country. So it seems we would not be able to satisfy the opposition no matter what we did. But the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), answers his own argument in his speech. He says that we have no reason for bringing in this legislation, yet at page 2666 of ' Hansard ' he says:
For some years back, I have been one of those who have found fault with the statistical information gathered by the Canadian government. A much better system might well be evolved and put in practice, instead of the present one which is neither accurate nor convenient. I believe that all the information which the Finance Minister, judging hy his remarks, desires, lie could obtain by the appointment of experts added to the departments of Trade and Commerce and Customs. There is no necessity for the appointment of a permanent Tariff Commission at all. You could appoint to the Customs and Trade and Commerce departments, expert technical men, who would get for you all the information which these commissioners are supposed to obtain. I believe that this would he a much less expensive way of arriving at more satisfactory results. These experts would he at work under the eyes of the minister and he responsible to him for their work, whereas the commission will be an irresponsible entity.
So that the hon. gentleman himself points out reasons for introducing this measure. The only contention of the hon. member is that the proper method of collecting information had not been adopted. Later on in his speech my hon. friend said:
Let him amend the Customs Act, if necessary, to make this change. I believe that both sides of the House would support an amendment to that effect. We do not begrudge any expense to get necessary information, hut we do not want legislation which will be a most radical departure from a cardinal principle of our constitution.
The junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said that he had suggested to the late government three years ago that a change should be made in the administration of the Customs Department, he bad suggested to the then Minister of Finance, (Mr. Fielding), that there should be established what he called a Tariff Bureau. I would like to know the difference between a Tariff Bureau and a Tariff Commission. It is a matter of name. He is going to establish a tariff tribunal to gather information and it seems to me a rose by any other name would smell just as sweet. Thus I say that these gentlemen have answered themselves when they say there is no reason for the appointment of this Tariff Commission.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said that the Minister of Finance in introducing this Bill had simply copied cheap Yankee legislation. He said:
The bill is largely an American model, nothing more or less than a cheap Yankee device.	.
The junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) says:
In the United States there is no such thing as a Tariff Commission, and there may never he-likely there never will be. Strictly speaking, there is no tariff board.
We have the hon. member for South Wellington saying that this Bill is an exact copy of something which the junior member for Halifax says does not exist. That is a peculiar state of affairs. Upon this point the hon. gentlemen have again answered themselves. The hon. member for South Wellington holds out a challenge to the Minister of Finance to disprove his statement that this proposed Tariff Commission will have the effect of increasing the tariff and that it was introduced for that purpose. If I thought the institution of the present Tariff Commission was being placed before this House and passed by this House for the purpose of increasing the tariff of this country at all times and would not be used also for the purpose of reducing the tariff, I for one would vote against it, and it is not fair to say that because a Tariff Commission was passed in the United States and because a protectionist party happened to be in power, therefore, the commission was created not only to preserve a high tariff in the United States, but to increase that tariff, because we know that in the last few years in the United States public opinion has been in favour of lowering the duties and that commission was appointed concurrently with

that feeling in the United States. I shall read the words of President Taft in his message to Congress, upon that particular measure, and see whether he thought that the creation of a Tariff Commission in the United States was intended for the purpose of increasing the tariff:
It is not unlikely that in the light of accurate statistics we may find that certain schedules in our tariff are too high. If we do, I shall at that time not hesitate to immediately recommend their revision. I believe the work of a tariff board should be to secure and present evidence, not to frame a tariff. With this evidence before it Conga-ess will act fairly and wisely and the United States have under this method, a tariff established on a thoroughly scientific basis, as it should have been a quarter of a century ago.
So that the challenge of the hon. member for South Wellington is answered by the President of the United States himself in a message upon the very subject of which my hon. friend was speaking.
Let me point out some other inconsistencies between the statements of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and the statements of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) at page 2662 of ' Hansard ' told us:
The fact therefore is that we are going to have three permanent tariff commissioners; a board just as permanently appointed as a bench of judges is appointed.
He entered a strong protest against the Bill because it created such a permanent tariff board. But, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) half an hour afterwards directed all his remarks to the importance of having a permanent tariff authority, and to ensure that permanency he urged that civil servants be selected to form a tariff bureau. What inconsistency there is between these gentlemen on the opposite side of the House! If only a few more of them would speak they would tear to shreds every argument they have used against this Bill. Then, we were told by gentlemen opposite that the appointment of this commission would have the effect of more closely allying the tariff with party government, and as a remedy against that the hon. member suggested that there should be officials taken from certain departments, officials under the control of the government, and to some extent depending for their promotion upon the minister, to form a ' tariff bureau ', and he contended this bureau would be freer from party bias than the board proposed under this Bill, which my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) said would be composed of men as independent as are the judges of the land. The fact " that hon. gentlemen opposite are driven to such a line of argument shows the weakness of their case. The three gentlemen Mr. MIDDLEBRO
who have spoken on the other side of the House usually present good strong reasons to support their views, and the fact that their arguments in the present instance are so illogical and so inconsistent simply shows that they have been casting around aimlessly for some contention to buttress their objections to this Bill. Then, the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) referring to the probable appointments to the tariff board stated that there was no doubt but that the appointees would be Conservatives. Well, so long as we have party government in this country, so long will the party in power favour its own friends, other things being equal. We might as well accept that idea as a start. It is a principle of party government that the party in power should appoint officials in whom they have confidence. Suppose, for example, that after we had been returned to power at the last election by an overwhelming majority on the principle of moderate protection, and on the principle of sustaining our tariff substantially as it is, except with such variations as are necessary from time to time, and that then we should turn around and appoint three free traders on this tariff commission, would any one suppose that we would be carrying out the mandate of the people and doing our duty to those who trusted us to administer the affairs of the country? No, we would be guilty of a breach of faith. However, that may be, I want to remind the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kyte) that it is not true that in all cases this government has followed _ the practice of appointing only its own friends. Why, the very minister who introduced this Bill comes from the ranks of his own party, and the man whom this government placed at the head of the Transcontinental Railway Commission is a Liberal. It will therefore be seen that although we have the right, if we choose, to appoint party friends, we have so far exercised our best judgment in calling to the various public positions men who we think can best administer public affairs in the true interest of the country. Another reason why we are introducing this Bill is to carry out a promise made by the Conservative party when in opposition, and this government believes in implementing its promises, although, I hope it will not cost us as much to implement our promises as it cost the late government to implement its guarantee to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Let us look at some of the duties which will be cast upon this new tariff board. It will be one of their first duties T presume to consider each item in the tariff. Now, I have given a little attention to this tariff for my own satisfaction, and I am free to say that I know very little about it, although possibly I do know as

much about it as mo3t hon. members in this House. Here is the tariff and I find there are three thousand seven hundred different articles dutiable and free in schedule A, and these again are grouped into seven hundred and ten items, so it is pretty safe to say there is not a single member in this House who knows what every item in that tariff is. It is also safe to hazard the assertion that not one half the members of this House know where the products come from, the local conditions of production, the cost of transportation, and what the duty is or what it ought to be. This board will be composed of specialists competent to study the tariff, and, as we know, this is an age of specialists. Every man who comes to the government urging a change in the tariff is a specialist in his own line, and when he appears before the minister to urge his case he necessarily has an advantage over tile minister because he has studied his own special line of business and knows what suits his own heeds. It is quite apparent that the time has come when we must have some regularly constituted body with proper powers of investigation, in order that we may intelligently legislate with respect to tariff matters. Under present conditions, some one walks into the office of the Minister of Finance or some deputation complains that the tariff is too high on a certain article and another comes in and says the tariff is too low. A deputation waits on the Minister of Finance urging him either to lower or to increase the tariff and that deputation presents arguments from every standpoint in favour of their request, and as to the accuracy of these statements the Minister of Finance of course has no assurance. Is it not well to have such a board as is now proposed to advise the minister; to seek information and to present a well considered and carefully thought out report to him? Let me give you an example of what I mean. Within the past few weeks there came from my own riding two deputations, one of them being on behalf of the Coal Association of the province of Ontario. That deputation pointed out to the Minister of Finance what was news to me, that if a vessel loads with coal at the town of Owen Sound and sails for Port Arthur, touching at an International port en route she does not have to pay duty on that coal; but, if the same vessel loads coal at Owen Sound and does a coasting business, and does not touch at an international port she has to pay a duty vof fifty-three cents per ton on that coal. That case is brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance, and of course the Minister of Finance cannot be expected to know all the circumstances and conditions which made that imposition of duty in the one case imperative, and in the other not. Such a case as that would be a 85
matter for the consideration of a Tariff Commission.
This body of experts would be able to take evidence on that. That certainly has the effect of diverting trade through international waters, because in one case there is a duty of 53 cents a ton on coal and in the other case there is no duty.
Then, the cement manufacturers may come down here. In my town there are three cement companies, and I understand the west desires a reduction of -the duty on cement, because the people in the west are complaining that the price of and duty on cement are too high. They say that a cement merger has been formed and is paying on watered stock a dividend which is equal to 25 or 30 per cent on its legitimate stock. These cement gentlemen cofne down here' and say, the price of cement is high, not because of the tariff, but because of the high freight rates between the east and the west. This commission has power to investigate both the cost of production and the cost of transportation to the west. In the State of Kansas there is a cluster of mills turning out cement which undersells to a great extent the cement produced in this country, and what is the reason? It is because they employ the cheap labour of the Latin races from Europe to whom they pay a lower rate of wage than our people will accept. In addition, alongside of the cement mills are silk mills in which the women of these Latin races work, so that the combination of the two makes it possible for these people to live on a rate of wages which would be ruinous to the workingmen of this country. These are matters which this commission will take into consideration. They are stated to me as facts, but I do not know whether they are facts or not. Therefore, I want the commission to take evidence and find out.
Then we had the fruit growers coming down here and saying that any lowering of the duties on fruits would be injurious to them, and you heard the answer of the late Prime Minister to the effect that he did not know whether the representations made were true or not, and that as reciprocity was on the tapis he could do nothing. The grain growers of the west also came here with their representations. The farmers of Ontario came saying that they were injured by the introduction of cheap American pork, and asked to have the duty on pork increased. Was any man in this House able to say definitely and accurately whether or not those duties should be increased, without some authoritative statement from a body of experts such as that proposed by this Bill? I could go on and illustrate by references to many other things. Take the Combines



Act. If a deputation comes to this House and says, we believe there is a combine in this country, in a certain article, by reason of which the price of that article has been unduly enhanced, who in this House knows whether that is the case or not? This commission has power to go right into the factories and investigate their books and bring the men before them and do anything else necessary to see whether the price has been unlawfully enhanced or not.
The next argument presented to the House by our hon. friends opposite is that the passage of this Bill would subvert the constitution of this country. I will admit that if there is anything in this Bill which gives legislative or executive action to the Tariff Commission, that argument is perfectly sound. I myself would vote against giving this commission any legislative or executive action with respect to the alteration or revision of the tariff. But the whole argument of hon. gentlemen opposite is based on an assumption which does not exist, and which would lead me to believe that they had prepared their speeches on this Tariff Commission, in the expectation that it would have some legislative or executive action. My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) referred to the resolution that was" moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the last Imperial Conference, which he said bore mo analogy to the functions of this commission. If the hon. gentleman had read that resolution, I think he would not have made that statement. What was the resolution that Sir_ Wilfrid Laurier mowed on that occasion. It was one praying that the Imperial Government would appoint a conn-mission composed not only of representatives of Canada, but of representatives ofv every other portion of the empire, and of Great Britain as well, to do exactly what this Tariff Commission is going to do. I will read that resolution:
He asked for the appointment of a Royal Commission with a view of investigating and reporting upon the natural resources of each rrart of the empire represented at this ."on-ference, the development attained and attainable, and the facilities for production, manufacture, and distribution; the trade of each part with the others and with the outside world, the food and raw material requirements of each, and the sources thereof available. To that extent, if any, the trade between each of the different parts has been affected by existing legislation in each, either beneficially or otherwise.
That commission was to do nothing but investigate and report, just what is proposed for this commission. Was there any question of the subversion of Canadian autonomy when the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition, and who is supposed to be the omnipresent protector Mir. MIDDLEBRO.
and vigilant mentor of Canadian autonomy, moved this resolution at the last Imperial Conference ? Yet the cases are exactly analogous, because that commission was simply asked to go and investigate facts and report, just as the commission now proposed is to do.
I wish also to refer to the Railway Commission, which hon. gentlemen opposite [DOT]appointed when in power. We have no fault to find with them for that; on the contrary, we have commended their action in that respect time and again, and so have the people of this country-why? Because there was a time not long ago when all the duties performed by the Railway Commission were performed by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council- more or less of a political body. But there came a time in the development of Canada when, by reason of the -development of our railways, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council could not attend to the many questions brought before it, and it became necessary, in the -interests of this country, that railway rates and everything pertaining to railways -should be assigned to a commission; and that commission was given -powers greatly in excess of those given to this commission.
This commission will only have power to-investigate and report. It would never do to give it the right and the power to do anything which would affect the revenues of the country. We are giving it much less power than we gave the Railway Commission. To the Railway Commission we gave power, not to do anything that would affect the revenues of the country, but to control the railway freight and passenger rates throughout the whole Dominion; and1 in that respect we gave them executive power and took from ourselv-es the right to have anything to say in fixing traffic rates on railways. Yet, although when we vested in the Railway Commission this sole-executive power to deal with railway rates, hon. gentlemen opposite had nothing to say but on the contrary fathered that proposition; now, when we are about to appoint a commission which will simply have the power to investigate and ascertain the facts-, and will not have any executive power at all, we are charged with subverting the constitution. Can hon. gentlemen opposite really realize the meaning of their words when they make such an argument?
The late First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) consented to the appointment of a Waterways Commission. He appointed t-hree commissioners. For what purpose? To ascertain the facts and conditions in connection with the international waters between this -country and the United States. But why did he appoint special commissioners for that purpose? Because the right hon. gentleman -and the late government

came to the conclusion that the subject of the international waters and the various encroachments on the Tights of the Dominion in that connection, were so complex and abstruse that the ministers of the late government had not the time to deal with them, and, therefore, they appointed an International Waterways Commission, whose duty it was to investigate into all the circumstances, conditions and facts and report. What were they authorized to do- their duties are defined in their first report in 1905 as follows:
Whose duty it shall be to investigate and report upon the conditions and uses of the waters adjacent to the boundary lines between the United States and Canada, including all of the waters of the lakes and rivers whose natural outlet is by the River St. Lawrence to the Atlantic ocean; also upon the maintenance and regulation of suitable levels, and also upon the effect upon the shores of these waters and the structures thereon, and upon the interests of navigation by reason of the diversion of these waters from or change in their natural flow; and, further, to report upon the necessary measures to regulate such diversion, and to make such recommendations for improvements and regulations as shall best subserve the interests of navigation in said waters. The said commissioners shall report upon the advisabilty of locating a. dam at the outlet of Lake Erie, with a view to determining whether such dam will benefit navigation, and if such structure is deemed necessary shall make recommendations to their respective governments looking to an agreement or treaty which shall provide for the construction of the same, and they shall make am estimate of the probable cost thereof.
Our hon. friends opposite will see that the late government gave that International Waterways Commission more powers than we are proposing to give this Tariff Commission, because they gave the Waterways Commission power to make regulations respecting international waters. This will be seen by reference to page 90 of the International Waterways Teport and carry them into executive action.
In due course by a report of the Committee of the Privy Council of Canada, approved by the Governor General of Canada, it was resolved : That His Majesty's government accept the invitation to co-operate in the formation of a commission. This report, after further reciting that as the subject to be dealt with pertained to ' the regulations of the waters adjaoent to the international boundary,' the matter, in so far as Canada was concerned, should he under the Department of the Interior and the Department of Public Works.
On the following page ol that report will be found the following:
After the appointment of the Canadian commissioners, the Postmaster General of Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in communicating the matter to the Canadian House of Com-85J
mons, in January last, dealt with the subject-matter of the commission as covering all waters adjacent to the boundaries of the two countries, and in the course of his speech made the following statements: In sections of the country where the boundary is not water, hut land, there are streams and large rivers which have their sources in one country and which flow into another. Complaint has been made by the United States that Canadians have constructed some works upon rivers which have their sources in Canada and which flow into the United States, and that these works affect the flow of the waters^ in their country. We also have made oomplaints to the United States that Americans have constructed upon some rivers, the St. John river, for instance, works which affect the flow of the waters in our country. It is, therefore, to the mutual interest and advantage of both countries to have the question properly investigated with a view of having concurrent legislation, if such should be found necessary.
For these reasons we have thought it advisable to respond to the invitation of the United States to have this question investigated. We have agreed to a commission to he composed of six members, three to represent the government of the United States and three to represent the government of Canada.
Did it ever occur to any hon. gentleman opposite to object that by establishing that Waterways Commission and giving it the powers we did, the late government was in any way subverting the constitution or taking from this parliament any of the poweTs which justly belong to it? Not one of them raised any such objection, but on the contrary, the Bill establishing that commission was supported without dissent, because parliament desired that the government should obtain the uest information available before deciding on any definite action. Then there was the International Fisheries Commission. Why did we appoint that? Let me here say that if there is anything in the argument hon. gentlemen opposite put forward against the appointment of a Tariff Commission, that argument would apply with still greater force against the appointment of any international commission. Because in the case of a Tariff Commission, this government has absolute control, whereas in the case of an International Commission, there are two governments concerned, each of which has as much say as the other. The government, in the ease of the Tariff Commission, may remove the commissioners from office and abolish the commission, but it cannot in the case of an International Commission, which is the outcome of a treaty, without going to Great Britain and consulting the Imperial authorities.
Why did the late government appoint an International Fisheries Commission? Because of the disputes which arose in connection with our fisheries. Some people wanted nets of a certain size, the people of British Columbia wanted certain things

done, and our maritime provinces wanted other things done. The government then did what any other intelligent government would have done. They determined to place these matters in the hands of experts, who would call the parties interested before them, gather the facts, on oath if necessary, and enable the government to devise more executive and intelligent legislation than it otherwise could have done. I can point to commission after commission and ask hon. gentlemen opposite to show one essential difference between the powers given these various commissions I have named, and the one we are appointing today, except that we are not now giving the Tariff Commission such large powers as we have some of the others. Yet we are told that in appointing this Tariff Commission we are subverting our constitution. Why, if that be the case, our constitution must have been completely upset long ago by these hon. gentlemen opposite, and yet we seem to be getting along famously.
A little while ago the question of technical industrial education came up in this House, and my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), himself proposed that this government should do-what? That it should appoint a commission. What for? To visit the industrial centres of Canada, and the United States, gather all the information there obtainable, and then cross the water to the countries of Europe, and after having made all the investigation possible, report to this House. There was then no fear in my hon. friend's mind of our subverting the constitution by the appointment of such a commission. That idea never occurred to hon. gentlemen opposite until the Bill we are now discussing was submitted to the House. They then went into their little chambers and worried about what position they ought to take, and what opposition they could make, and they determined on a line of argument which does not do much credit to their intelligence.
My hon. friend the junior member for Halifax said: I do not care that this commission may not have legislative or executive power. When it brings in a report, that report is bound to be tinctured into the tariff. But does he not know that this commission is appointed simply to ascertain the facts, and you cannot get rid of the facts. You must have the facts in framing your tariff. Let my hon. friend look up the speech made by Mr. Champ Clark on the Bill which was amended by the United States Senate, and he will see that the leader of the Democrats and the advocate of low tariff reform in the United States, while he objected to the establishment of a commission, because it would be composed of Republicans, said that the Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
commission would not have legislative or executive power, but simply power to collate the facts and report; and he went on to say that facts are facts, no matter whence they come, and, therefore, he would not oppose the Bill. My hon. friend said this afternoon that the present government are in favour of higher protection. Nothing of the kind. Suppose the representation is made that the duty on agricultural implements are too high. Well, if they are too high I am in favour of lowering them, but I want some definite scientific information to prove this, and at present there is nobody, and no tribunal from which I can get that information. This Tariff Commission, however, will have the power to enter every factory, every industrial establishment, examine its books find out the cost of production, the amount of capital invested, the dividends paid, and all the conditions governing it, and then report the facts to the government. And on the reports of this commission, the government will come to a conclusion as to what tariff legislation is desirable. To my mind the objection to investigations of that kind should come rather from the manufacturers, and be prompted by a desire to conceal the facts from the country. As President Taft said, when speaking of the tariff board appointed under the Payne-Aldrich law: I do not say that this board should be established, because the tariff is too high or too low, but in order that we may ascertain the facts and revise our tariff if the facts call for a revision.
My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean), said on several occasions that there is not in other countries a Tariff Commission similar to this. Quite true, but they have other institutions for determining what the tariff shall be. What is the object of appointing those men? It is simply in order that we may get at the facts, because our tariff must be based on the facts.
Now, let me give another illustration of our lack of information in this House; and, if I refer to the reciprocity treaty, I do so in no controversial way, but in illustration of the need of actual information which we should have in the country, not only to assist us in revising our own tariff, but in negotiating commercial treaties with other countries. Last year, when the reciprocity matter was before the House, we were very anxious to get information as to the prices of commodities on the American side and on our own. In the debate on the 2nd of March, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster), said:
I would like to call the attention of the Finance Minister to the message sent by President Taft in reply to a request from the Senate, in which statistics are given as to

the different items affected by the schedule in the agreement now under discussion. These statistics include the prices of various commodities such as beef, pork, butter, Ac., in Canada and the United States for a series of years, especially for the last year. In reply to the request the President sent down a list which gave the exact information required by the Senate.
In reply, the Hon. Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, said:
Of course we had to use our own sources of information and hon. gentlemen who criticise the agreement will have to do likewise.
That is the only answer we got. Later on the present Prime Minister (Mr. Borden.) drew the matter to the attention of the then Minister of Finance, but the only information he received was that a document had been published by the Minister of Labour giving prices in Canada and labour conditions. But we all know that that document was not compiled with a view to the reciprocity treaty, but merely in connection with the work of the Department of Labour. And the hon. Mr. Fielding added:
There is no other information available.
The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) wrote to the Department of Trade and Commerce asking for information. Fur we must have information in a case of that kind if we are to give an intelligent decision upon a question whether such a treaty as was proposed should be approved or not. We must know, for instance, whether products affected by the treaty could be raised in a foreign country more cheaply than here and even adding transportation laid down here at a lower figure than they could be produced for in this country. And what reply did the hon. gentleman receive?
I beg to return you herewith your reference No. 172 for statement showing comparative prices of butter and eggs in London, England, and certain points in Canada and the United States. This department has no information upon the subject.
Imagine that! Imagine writing to the Department of Trade and Commerce for information that we ought to have in order to form an intelligent opinion upon a reciprocity pact and then only receive the answer, ' This department has no information !' Think of what this means, especially when on the other side of the line they had a body of trained experts who had been employed for years in collecting facts, so that when the United States government came to deal with this matter they had ' mountains of information '. Hon. Mr. Perle.y also wrote to the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce on the subject and. received this reply:
The compilation of statistics such as that requested in your return has more than once engaged the attention of this department, but we found that it required very considerable work which this department has yet been unable to undertake.
Not only that, but the then Minister of Finance told 'the people of this country that it was not necessary to have any information in order to negotiate the reciprocity pact. I will read you his speech to that effect. In this very same debate we were twitting hon. members who then sat on this side with having nothing to act upon except the blue-books which had been laid upon the table and which give us no intelligible information as to prices and conditions here as compared with those of the United States. Hon. Mr. Fielding said:
Then, with regard to what took place at Washington, I want to say to my hon. friends that we had abundance of statistics. We had the various documents and public books of the United States and Canada, to which we were able to refer from time to time, and we did not fail to make use of the ... I wish to add that in my judgment, the information for the purpose of this agreement, was not necessary at all.
Imagine that ! And the former Minister of Customs made a similar statement later on, as I will show. These gentlemen went there saying: We do not need information oar statistics such as have been compiled by the United States Tariff Commission; we can go down there and, without anything of that kind, negotiate a treaty with the President of the United States. I imagine the two representatives of Canada on one side of the conference table, and on the other side President Taft and some of the brainiest men. of the United States, armed with official information as to the prices, as to consumption of products and the extent of production on the American side, and on the Canadian side as well, which they have been collecting for years'. I can imagine the smile on the President's face when he found Mr. Fielding did not have, and apparently that he did not want, any information. And when these American representatives asked for concessions and Mr. Fielding gave them, they must have felt that it was like taking candy from children. The Canadian representatives went there without information, without any knowledge to guide them in what they were doing. On the other hand, the American representatives knew tile position exactly, their every move on the chessboard of that negotiation was made on definite, accurate, scientific information gathered by men who had been all over the United States and Canada and knew exactly the conditions in both countries. They knew exactly what they were doing, and we were playing the game like

a lot of children. And when the United States unwittingly threw out this lifebuoy, document 849, we grasped at it, and it helped to save us from national disaster. This document was one Of the most powerful arguments used by the Conservatives in the recent appeal to the people, for they were able to prove from it thut, oin the showing of the United States themselves, it would be injurious for this country to negotiate a treaty with the United States.
1 do not wonder that the bon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) does not want a Tariff Commission appointed, for it was the Tariff Commission of the United States which elicited facts which helped to turn the hon. gentleman's party out_ of power. I venture to say that had my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had a Tariff Commission in operation a year before, he would not have negotiated a treaty, and the chances are he would have been still on this side of the House. That is one of the most cogent arguments I can give for having authentic information on which we could base an intelligent conclusion.
Now, by way of digression, let me show the hind of information that these gentlemen in the United States collected. I refer first to the paper schedules. I find there are fifty schedules with respect to the paper manufacturing industry alone. And, be it noted, there is not a single recommendation in this report. They do not say to the President of the United States: It is better to do so and so. If our commission were to do likewise, I should object to it, because it is not for them to make suggestions for legislative action. Their message should be: Here are the facts; use your own sweet will upon them. So, in this document No. 849, there is neither suggestion nor recommendation as to what should be done in view of the facts collected, simply 127 pages of official facts with respect to reciprocity with Canada. Can any one find fault with that? And as to this department of pulp and news-print paper,' as showing the scope of the investigation, they say:
The data on pulp and paper included in the following tables was secured from 42 ground-wood mills, 17 sulphite mills, and 27 news-print mills, making a total of 86 mills and representing about two-thirds of the ground wood-pulp and news-print paper production of the United States and all of the sulphite pulp used in the production of newsprint paper. An investigation of the cost of production in all the other mills is now under way. The data from Canada were taken from a number of mills producing over two-thirds of the total output of news-print paper in the Dominion, including the best equipped mills . . . All these figures, including those from Canada, have been [DOT][DOT]secured directly by our representatives from the hooks of the different companies. We prepared exact schedules including all essential items of Mr. MIDDLEBRO. [DOT]
equipment, cost, and wages; and for each of the companies included in the tables, we have the original schedules covering all the items in detail.
An absolutely thorough investigation of the whole industry. Now, take the wool schedule, and let us see what investigation they made of the question of sheep raising, the basic industry for wool:
Coming to sheep, we approach a phase of agricultural production that has for several months past been a subject of a painstaking inquiry at the hands of the Tariff Board. We refer to that particular branch of live stock husbandry underlying schedule K of the United States tariff, to wit, the growing of sheep in the various countries and the conditions surrounding the marketing of flock products. This inquiry, necessarily worldwide in its bearing, is not completed. We are nevertheless, able to speak at the present time with a reasonably complete knowledge of the facts concerning the sheep growing industry in the United States and Canada, more especially as relates to comparative conditions in Ontario and such typical states as Ohio, Pennsylvania and Michigan. Representatives of the board have visited some 700 typical farms in the leading sheep breeding sections of Ohio, south Virginia, western Pennsyvania, west Virginia, New Hampshire and Vermont, obtaining facts and figures covering costs and prices. These data are now being analysed and worked out with a view toward developing cost of wool production. In connection therewith the cost of maintenance of sheep per head for a year in Ohio and adjacent states has already been developed. The method pursued in obtaining first hand information as to the cost of keeping sheep was through schedules filled out by exnerts who personally visited the farms studied.
The accompanying tables show the result of a study of two Ohio counties so investigated, and the data presented may be taken as fairly indicating the cost of maintaining sheep in the localities most largely interested. These figures are tentative, and are subject to revision and possible correction when the entire investigation has been completed.
I quote that to show the thoroughness with which that commission made the investigation. The woollen industry in Ontario to-day is in a decaying condition. Would it not be proper for this commission to examine, after the manner of the United States Tariff Commission, the conditions in Ontario, and in that thorough manner? I think if we can rejuvenate the woollen trade of this country, that is one instance of what this Tariff Commission might do.
Now, Sir, I want to summarize what I think should be the duties of this commission.
(a)	Will be a medium of gathering accurate and definite information on production, transportation and prices of goods at home and abroad, without which there can he no intelligent legislation in tariff matters.

(b)	This information may be obtained on oath and the production and inspection of the books of any concern to prove or disprove the need of protection or bonuses.
(c)	In so far as jurisdiction is conferred on the commission it will tend to remove the tariff from party politics and transfer it to a semi-judicial body but rightly giving it no executive legislative powers to affect our revenues.
(d)	It will provide a long felt want, a body of experts on our tariff and on conditions of production at home and abroad.
(e)	Will enable the Governor in Council through its medium to decide whether, or not there exists any combine or agreement under section 12 Customs Act, 1907, and to remove or lower the duties on all articles unduly enhanced in price because of such combine.
(f)	Will be able to ascertain definitely and report whether or not goods are being dumped into Canada contrary to the dumping clause of our Customs Act and if so to enable the government to have the 15 per cent added.
(g)	They can prepare special reports of the cause of the decline in certain industries or in certain branches of agriculture, or trade with other countries, and the changes and effect and operation of the tariff of, or treaties with other nations; on the trade and industries of Canada.
(h)	Consolidate the many Tariff Acts, Schedules, orders in council in Canada and our commercial treaties with other nations and compile and publish a glossary on our own tariffs or as President Taft said of their own, to translate it into plain English, and save to a great extent the employment of customs brokers and the worry of importers and others in adjusting duties.
I think these conclusions cover probably what would be the principal duties of this commission. For this and other reasons I have given, I have much pleasure in supporting the Bill.

We had supposed that we had constitutional government, but I think we can consider now that we are henceforth to be governed by commission. While we have appointed a good many commissions, we have also dispensed with the services of some. I would like to call the attention of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) to the fact that while the government has seen fit, as a measure of economy, to dispense with the services of three commissioners appointed for the purpose of supervising the construction of the Transcontinental railway, the money that they are going to save in that measure of economv thev are going to lose now by the appointment of the proposed Tariff Commission. So if my hon. friend is that
friend of economy which he poses as being, he will vote with this side of the House against the second reading of the Bill. It is not economy, I think, either in the matter of the expenditure of money or in the efficiency of the public service, to dispense with three commissioners charged with the responsibility of constructing a work of the most essential advantage to the country, at an expenditure of many millions of dollars, an expenditure that requires the most careful supervision in order to secure satisfactory results. But it is right and proper on grounds of economy and efficiency to dispense with the three Transcontinental Railway Commissioners, then there are no grounds of economy, and I think it has already been shown no grounds of efficiency, for the appointment of the proposed Tariff Commission-three commissioners, at a salary equal to that of the cabinet ministers who appoint them, with a secretary whose salary is equal to that of the Deputy Ministers of the various departments up to a year or two ago.
However, it has been decided by the government to appoint this commission, and we must assume that there is a purpose in the appointment. It cannot be presumed that even a very lavish government would appoint a commission at an initial salary cost of $24,500 a year, and with the almost unlimited expenses that will follow, without a purpose, a purpose I am confident beyond the mere finding of positions at comfortable salaries for their friends.
If I understand the matter, the commission is to be appointed for the purpose of securing information upon which to base changes in the tariff. I heard the Prime Minister discussing that subject, and it seemed to me he wished the House to understand that this commission was appointed merely for the purpose of collecting statistics. But I cannot think, as I have said, that even a lavish government would appoint a $25,000 commission merely for the purpose of collecting statistics. There must be a purpose beyond the mere collection of statistics, and flip purpose I think is to be found upon the information collected changes in the tariff. Unless that hp the purpose, then there ;- no purpose that would justify the appointment.
The purpose of the commission, as I understood the Finance Minister in his speech and as I understand those, who have spoken on the same side on behalf of the Bill, and as I understand the contents of the Bill itself, is to find reasons -I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker-to find excuses for increases in the tariff, to find out to what extent the tariff can be increased while the people may still be induced to submit to these increased exac-

tions and retain our hon. friends in office.
I quite agree that if there is to be tariff changes it is necessary that there should be information, that there should be inquiry; but in my humble judgment the purpose of the inquiry should be the direct opposite of that which has been indicated from the other side of the House, and by the terms of the Bill. I understand that the revenues of Canada are some twenty or thirty millions of dollars in excess of the needs of expenditure. It would seem to me that there might very well be inquiry as to a readjustment of the tariff whereby the burden of this extra taxation might be removed from the shoulders of the people, and as to such a readjustment of the tariff burden that it would bear more equally upon the wealth and upon the labour of our people. There might be a further inquiry as to how far the present tariff conditions tend to divert the payments made by the consumer into private pockets rather than into the public treasury. If these were the purposes of the appointment of the commission I could understand its propriety.
At the present time the business conditions of this country are exceedingly favourable. The Minister of Finance suggested in his sipeech that such a time was not the time to make changes in the tariff. I would respectfully submit that if the changes to be made are to be made along the lines that I would wish to see, ' at such a time ' is the time to make the changes. The present boom condition in our country is good for the man who has nothing; because he meets opportunity to better his position; and it is good for the man who has much because he meets opportunity to make that much more; but in the interests of the 75 per cent or maybe 80 per cent of the people who have practically fixed incomes, the farmers, the salaried employees or the wage labourers, to whom these opportunities do not come by reason of these good limes but upon whom the high cost of living bears exceedingly and to a greater and greater degree from year to year, it seems to me it would be well worthy of consideration if some part of the burden of the $75,000,000 of our revenue that is raised by customs taxation might not, under some readjustment of the tariff, be lessened to reduce the cost of living and so better the circumstances of that 75 per cent of our people.
If the commission to be appointed were to be composed of men holding the well recognized and differing views which are held in regard to customs taxation, and if the members of the commission would loyally represent all the various interests affected, the consumer as well as the producer, and if the evidence as secured were made available to the public and were secured for that purpose, then the proposed Mr. OLIVER.
commission would be a commission in fact as well as in name. But the men whom it is proposed to appoint will be political and tariff partisans. The commission _ will act as directed by the minister and will report only to him. It will be a commission in name and in cost but not a commission in fact. As I understand the matter this is a commission to humbug the people into believing that the information being gathered is being gathered in the public interest when really it is being gathered in special interests at the public expense.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. gentleman that it is not permissible to impute improper motives.

I beg pardon, Mr. Speaker, I am not imputing motives to any person in the House, it is the legislation to which I am imputing motives as I think I am permitted to do.
To me it seems that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) disputes with the hon. the Postmaster General the position of humourist of the Cabinet. It is surely a joke that $24,500 of the people's money, with unlimited expenses, is to be taken in the people's name for the purpose of securing information which will enable the special interests the 'better to rob the people by means of tariff changes.
But there is a particularly creamy joke contained in subsection 3 of section 4 of the Bill. This clause provides authority by which the commission may hold inquiries into combines which are alleged to enhance prices. The provision reads:
' In the same manner as a judge of the Exchequer Court or any other judge, therein referred to, may be so empowered.'
The men appointed as political partisans to do certain work in justification of party policy, under the direction of, and reporting to the Minister of Finance, are to have the same standing as to inquiries concerning the combines to whom the government owes its existence, as a judge of any court.
I notice that the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Amesj laid1 some stress upon the necessity of tariff legislation that would protect the labourer. Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the labourer, thie man whose capital is his labour and who must sell that capital in order to live, is in exactly the same position as the producer who depends upon the export market for the price of his products. The farmer who depends upon the export market must sell in competition with the world; and the labourer, even in the most highly protected country must sell his labour just the same in competition with the world. There is protection for the capital invested in the industries, but there is no protection for the labour that is the industriy.

It is a fact that the labourer is from time to time urged to vote for a high tariff, and it is a fact that up to the present and generally speaking he has done so; but it is not on the promise of higher wages, it is on the threat of the closed factory.
The demand for labour depends, not upon the tariff, but upon t'he market for the product of the factory, and the higher the tariff the greater the restriction on the demand for the product and therefore the greater the restriction on the demand for labour. At the_ same time, every increase in the tariff increases the cost of living to the labourer. The promises or the suggestions of benefit to the labouring classes from high tariffs have never been fulfilled and they never will be fulfilled.
The government was elected in opposition to the policy of reduction of taxation and expansion of trade. The defection of the high tariff section of the Liberal party represented in the Cabinet by the Minister of Finance aided most materially in achieving the success of the government. The interests elected the government; they are entitled to their pound of flesh and are demanding it. Admittedly it must be difficult for a government elected on the cry ' let well enough alone,' to accede to the demands of the interests on such short notice, or, in other words, to deliver the goods. But, this Tariff Commission will lay the wires through which the power will be turned on a little later.
In the meantime the interests will be kept quiet and the people will not be alarmed. If the government believes that industry can be built up and resources developed by maintaining or increasing the burden of taxation and by maintaining or increasing the restrictions on trade, they have the mandate of the people to give effect to their views. No doubt they will need a great deal of information, but it is for them to get their information by the ordinary means taken under a responsible system of government. They were elected to increase taxation and restrict trade, let them now do what they asked a mandate to enable them to do-, and not seek by subterfuge of miscalled commissions to shirk full responsibility for their policy and its result.

It is no small compliment to the merits of the legislation now before the House that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) usually the most belligerent of the opposition, glorying in strife and in his happiest mood when the strife is hottest, should be under the necessity of artificially creating the little enthusiasm he did, and that a man of his capacity and his power of language should be under the necessity of, in attacking this Bill, reading
from carefully prepared sophisms, and attacking what his friends call a radical measure by excerpts from the radical press. The hon. member for Edmonton, of all men, is at his best in opposition.
If a flaw can be found in the Bill, he is the one to find it; if there is an evil present or to be anticipated, he is the one to reveal it. But, Sir, he has laboured, as he never laboured in this House before, in his attempt to attack the Bill to create a tariff board. I favour this Bill; the hon. member for Edmonton opposes it. Why does he oppose it? If I can grasp that part of his address which dealt with the Bill, he opposes it first because it is expensive-because he says it will cost something over $24,500 a year. That is the annual expense of a tariff board that is to lay the foundation facts for a fiscal policy which collects annually some $73,000,000 of revenue. The hon. gentleman made no comparative references to other countries. He made no comparative reference to the present cost in our country to show that we are going to incur any more expense than we have done before. Nor did he make any attempt to show that the method now adopted is not as good as and not much better than the one we have had hitherto. So it is impossible to say how his argument ended, if it can be called an argument at all. He then went on to say that now was a golden opportunity to reduce the tariff, because we are in prosperous times. Yet he was a member of a government which entrusted the tariff to a Minister of Finance, who for ten years propounded to the House the very opposite argument-that while times were prosperous, while things were going well, the less we interfered with the tariff the better. But the exigencies of opposition necessarily produce anomalies, and, therefore, we need not be surprised at the hon. gentleman finding himself now compelled to conflict with -his own policy as a member of the previous government, and to present an argument that destroys the very theory on which that government acted.
I support this Bill, and for the simplest of all reasons, because in my judgment it goes to improve the public service. I can conceive of no other purpose in the Bill. There is no other purpose evident on its face and I can see no ghost behind it. I believe it will work out to the improvement of the public service. The task of framing a tariff in this country has been committed to this parliament by the voice of the people at every general election since there was a Canada, and never more pronouncedly than in the last general election. In that task I can see no divisions. That duty is one, and indivisible, and that duty belongs to the parliament of Canada. But,

Sir, that duty is great, and in proportion as it is great, for at every step in its performance we affect vitally the well-being of every citizen of this country; and in proportion as the responsibility for its right performance is great, in that degree should we take care that we come to its performance armed at every point and well prepared. This Bill provides the means for that preparation; it does nothing more; and it provides the means that seem to me to be suited to the immensity of the undertaking. It provides a means that can expand with the certain expansion of our industrial life.
I support the Bill because whatever this parliament has to do, if it is worth doing at all, is worth doing well, and I believe the commission to be appointed will assist us in the performance of our duty. But surely the hon. member for Edmonton and every other hon. member who has spoken can distinguish between the responsibility for the performance of duty and the procuring of means by which a duty can be well performed.
Now, this measure is opposed by His Majesty's loyal opposition, and why? There have been up to this time four hon. members on their feet, and I apprehend, from the conclusion of the arguments which they presented, that it was decided in the councils of the opposition, largely now composed of vacant chairs, that of the two evils, acceding to or opposing this Bill, the latter was the better one to choose. There was likely much disputing, and much violent disputing if we may judge from the confused and conflictm? arguments presented; but when a party addresses itself to the task of engaging the allegiance of two opposite schools of thought by presenting to each of them principles that mutually destroy each other, and arguments that are mutually destructive, when that is the purpose of a party's being then we must expect anomalies and absurdities in its attitude in parliament. The first ground the opposition took was this, that there was no mandate from the country for this Bill. None of them assumed the position that there was no purpose to he served by it. One and all can see that correct and sufficient data for the framing of a tariff are a necessity, and a great one. No one would assert that we have had those data before. Hon. gentlemen opposite have evidently been taught a lesson by the last election. They have evidently learned, from the quandary in which they found themselves, when confronted with the great mass of data in the United States as against our own, when discussing the reciprocity pact; and therefore not one of them has stood in his place in the House and argued that there was not a necessity in this country for more elaborate, complete and scientific data as a foundation for tariff revision.

But they say there is no mandate for this commission. Why, the right hon. leader of the government on 40 or 50 platforms has advocated it in specific terms, and has specifically promised it if returned to power. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) stated that he himself had heard the right hon. leader of the government on more than one occasion advocate this, but briefly. Now, there is no doubt that it was presented as a more or less prominent feature of the programme o' the late opposition; it was laid before this country for its acceptance or rejection; the electorate of Canada came to the polls and signed the contract for its acceptance, and now we are asked to violate that contract. If a specific pledge of a united party prior to an election accepted by the people is not a mandate, then I ask my hon. friends how can a mandate be given? But I ask further, if a Tariff Commission had not been specificially advocated in the platform of the leader of the party prior to the election-if indeed nothing had been said of it-the people of this country have certainly entrusted the Conservative party with the task of framing a tariff. The people have certainly entrusted parliament and the government with the task of framing a tariff, and in so committing that task they give an implied mandate to the government to take the best means to carrying out that work. So that I say such an implied mandate would itself be sufficient even if a specific pledge had not been actually proffered and accepted.
What is the next objection to this Tariff Commission? It is that we could get the same information from officials in the department and that if, instead of taking officers immediately under the wing of the minister we choose to appoint a commission, we are thereby raising a barrier between the people and the government. Well, I can see no difference in principle between the gathering of information by a commission specially appointed for that purpose and obtaining it from officers directly under the control of the minister. But I can see a great difference in the practicability and thoroughness of the one method as compared with the other. In the one case we have a body of men specially appointed for the purpose of investigation and specially qualified, and divorced in proper measure from the control of the minister in chaTge. These men are appointed to do specific work and are responsible for the duality of the work they do. I should think, therefore, that we could obtain much better results from the work of a commission of that kind than from officials in the Customs Department who could neither be specially trained for that purpose nor have the same facilities for doing the

work. It, therefore, seems to me that hon. gentlemen opposite are simply beating the air when they quote Bourinot and American constitutional precedents to show that this parliament is divesting itself of responsibility when it authorizes the government to employ a commission of experts in order that it may be put in possession of the facts and the information that is required on which to base tariff legislation. This is all the Bill does.
Then hon. gentlemen opposite proceed to argue that there is an evil spirit behind this measure that the ghost of' high protection is behind it, and that it is part of a scheme by which the government hope to evade responsibility for imposing a high tariff on this country. My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) said that the battle is now on between the moderate and the high protectionists of Canada. Well, I can assure my hon. friend, if that would give him any, encouragement, that if the battle is on between the moderate and the high protectionists, he will find me in the army of the moderates. But where does he see the gauntlet for that battle in the Bill before us. We are told that the ghost of high protection is stalking around this measure because in the United States, which is a country of high protection, there is a Tariff Board. They say there is a Tariff Board in Japan, one in Germany and another in France, and that all these countries are protective. But when the hon. gentleman opposite cites France, Germany, Japan and the United States as countries having Tariff Boards, he should remember that these countries are the advance guard in the industrial progress of the world.
German statesmen at one time belonged to the school now represented in this House by the lonely member for Red DeeT (Mr. Clark 1. Prince Bismarck was one who once belonged to the school my hon. friend represents in Canada, but after look-ink over the world, after looking especially into the record of the United States, he said that the history of that great republic was a lesson to him in industrial progress, and he thought that Germany ought to benefit by that lesson. He, therefore, in 1878 a year that is also historic in Canadian annals, abandoned free trade in Germany, and gave that country a protective policy. To-day Germany is the leader of the world in industrial growth. It has seen fit to introduce business methods into the conduct of its national affairs-. It has delegated to well qualified individuals the task of collecting -data on which to base legislation. That is a task we are giving to this Tariff Commission in order that it may collect and collate all the information and data possible and submit the same to the minister responsible so that
he may, in his tariff legislation, carry out the will of the people. Other European countries are moving in the same direction. Hon. gentlemen opposite say to us:	We
do not want you to collect the facts, we do not want you to have data collected by this independent commission which you can submit to the people in order to show that the tariff you put in force is a just one. I do not wonder that hon. gentlemen opposite should take that position. For years back the Liberal party has_ been an organized anomaly as regards its fiscal policy. There are in that_ party whole squadrons of men whose opinions are diametrically opposed on fiscal questions. The only cement that keeps them together is their opposition to the government. _ Now, we must either embody the _ principle of protection in our tariff or eliminate it. Has any hon. gentleman opposite declared that he would eliminate it? Would the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) eliminate it? Would even he, representing a constituency in the far west eliminate that principle from onr tariff? He remains silent. Why, if he -did, by whom would he be opposed? He would be opposed at once by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) whose spineless amendment he now supports, and he wou.d be supported by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), possibly by some others who think that a certain local sentiment in their constituencies would back them up And he would have the support of a section of the electors of this country who still harbour the free trade theory. These two sections are both sitting together in the opposition, both clinging to principles which cannot live together. And, while that conflict of opinion obtains among hon. gentlemen opposite they must necessarily assume absurd positions in this House. I have often felt sympathy for the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who leads the opposition. For between the two factions that he leads, the directly opposite schools, the right hon. gentleman has been pitchforked for twenty years, between free trade doctrines on the one side and the protectionist doctrinaires on the other, until finally he landed without any opinion at all. And the right hon. gentleman, in order to lead a party that endeavours to combine irreconcilables, has been compelled to acknowledge to the people of Canada that, between the free trade theory and the protection theory he inclines neither to the one side nor to the other. On this side, of the House, as I have previously stated, if a war was on-as the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), and the hon. member foT Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), both devoutly hope-between the moderate protectionists and the high protectionists, I am
