on the side of the moderate protectionists. I believe that in this young country, with, for a long time at least, a far greater store of natural resources than we are able to bring to a developed state at home, we must, for some time at least, follow a protectionist policy. I also believe that the best objects of protection are served by a moderate tariff, by a policy that accedes to and recognizes the interests of all classes. I believe also that the interests which each section has in that policy are not in every sense equal or in every sense uniform. I believe that, under these circumstances, the proper policy is a policy of reasonable protection doing justice to the consumer, as well as to all others.
On agricultural implements, for instance.

Yes, as on everything else. And if my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will read the address I had the honour of delivering in this House in January, 1911, he will find that I stood then where I stand now; that I stated then-not in the same words perhaps, but in words with the same meaning-just what I state to-day. And I would remind those who see evil spectres behind this Bill, those who think that clause by clause and sentence by sentence it is quite innocuous but that there is something terrible, but all unseen in this measure presented by the government, let me remind them that the Board of Tariff experts in the United States has presented several specific reports to Congress and the president, and that every recommendation made by the president in pursuance of those reports has been in favour of a revision downwards; that the Tariff Board of the United States, as between the high and the moderate protectionists-if such exists over there-has favoured the moderate protectionists every time. But no report of that body, or of any other such body that pretended to economic intelligence, has ever favoured a policy of free trade there or here. So that, I should think, if hon. gentlemen opposite could see any light at all through the confusion that exists around them, they would favour this Bill especially if they are, as stated by the hon. member for Richmond, moderate protectionists. Because wherever the Tariff Board has operated it has brought about conditions of moderate, rather than high protection.
Now, Sir, I have stated concisely my reasons for supporting this Bill, and have endeavoured to meet what I conceive to be the arguments raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. If there is any that I have missed, I would like to hear it now. If there is not, I would like to know why these hon. gentlemen oppose this Bill. Of course, they are subject to the exigencies of party warfare; they want to look both Mr. MEIGHEN.
ways when the general election comes on. Unless they can say rightly or wrongly- that we are Haman's-gallows protectionists, they cannot say anything; and as they want to fight our tariff, be it good or bad, they feel they must oppose our tariff commission as well. That is practically the sole reason that animates the opposition. There can be no other.
Now, if our tariff is going to be made in a back room, if it is going to be made in the ante-room of the Stock Exchange, if it is going to be made in the private closet of a campaign committee, then I am willing to concede that the fewer facts that are presented to the public land to parliament, the better; for a system of that kind loves darkness rather than light. But, if the tariff is to be made to suit tire necessities of business and of all classes of business, farming included, if the circumstances that govern it are to be business circumstances and not party political circumstances, then the more facts we have the better, and the more light we have the better. Hon. gentlemen opposite did not frame their tariff upon, that principle. And, so far as' they altered it and revised it, or left it alone, as time went on and as circumstances and our industrial life developed, they were animated by this principle-if you call it a principle-that their course was dictated on the one hand by 'political friendship and on the other hand by political antipathy. If that is to be the guiding principle of the party in power we should have no Tariff Commission, and the smaller the body of facts we have the better. But folly is the very essence of such a tariff and disaster its result; and I concede the point that darkness is its 'best associate and ignorance is its only fortification. I commend the government in proposing this Bill, because it is a specific implementing of a specific promise to the Canadian people. I commend it because it promises to this country that we will endeavour to get method into our 'business legislation, such as people who succeed introduce into their own business affairs. I think this is. only a step. I do not think it will give ail the results that some anticipate from it. I know that its difficulties will be much greater than' many expect. But I believe that it will give some substantial results. And I believe that the principle embodied here, instead of being combatted should be extended from one department of our legislation to another until we should have more systematic and equitable laws throughout with results more generally suited to the conditions in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest and pleasure to my hon. friend, toe Minister of Finance, in his address in moving
the second reading of this Bill. I listened

with interest, because I am always anxious to know what an hon, gentleman means by a Bill he has introduced.
I was particularly interested to hear what arguments the' Finance Minister could use to justify the Bill. I listened with pleasure to the very clear, simple and excellent speech with which he moved the second reading of this Bill. I am one of those who at all times are willing to hear arguments; I am not anxious to hear arguments surcharegd with hot air from anybody or on any subject. Therefore I would not attach too much importance to the so-called arguments of some hon. gentlemen who have spoken since the Finance Minister on the other side of the House. They have not said much about the Bill, but they have had a lot to say about many other things. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have long been in favour of a statistical department in the Finance Department, well organized, for the purpose of collecting statistics and facts,, as hon. gentlemen opposite call them, to aSord information to the Finance Minister in compiling a tariff. I [think everybody in the House recognizes that the Finance Minister, no matter which party he belongs to, requires all the information he can get when he compiles a tariff. Therefore we are all united on that point. The question is which is the better way to get that information. My own opinion is that the best way to get it is by means of a statistical branch in connection with the Finance Department, or the Customs Department, something like the Insurance branch now belonging to the Finance Department. It has been said by an hon. member opposite, I think the hon. member for St. Antoine Montreal (Mr. Ames), that in 1907 when three ministers of the late government travelled through the country getting information for the purpose of compiling a tariff, their work amounted to a farce, or words to that effect; he said they gathered a lot of material that was absolutely impossible for them to digest. Now one strong argument in favour of a statistical branch in the Finance Department is that it would not take away the purpose the late ministers had in view in travelling through the country to get information. With all due deference to my hon. friends opposite, I think they will find that the people will insist on getting access to the minister himself, that is to say, interested parties will insist on seeing the minister himself. Therefore he will not get rid of the trouble, he will not be able to avoid interviews with various interests, by appointing tne proposed Tariff Commission. Nor do I think that he ought to refuse to see directly the various interests particularly interested in the tariff. Now when these three ministers belonging to the late government went through the country they
came in personal contact with the people most interested in the tariff; not only that, but they became acquainted with the country through which they travelled, they visited the factories, and they endeavoured to acquire information from the working man and the farmer. Now how many farmers and how many working men will the Finance Minister see if he sits in his office and depends entirely upon the reports of the Tariff Commission? I think, even with the Tariff Commission, it will still be necessary for the Finance Minister to visit various parts of the country and get his information at first hand. But if he had the aid of such a statistical branch in his department as I am advocating, he might be able to get rid of much of this trouble.
The Minister of Finance in introducing his Bill laid stress on the fact that it gave the Tariff Commissioners authority to examine people under oath, l'hat authority could also be given a statistical branch of the Finance Department; to summon witnesses and hear them under oath if they wished, and under Section 12 of the Tariff Act, the Governor in Council have that right, now on certain conditions arising. Parliament could easily authorize the Finance Department or any other department to examine witnesses under oath in matters pertaining to the tariff. The hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal, (Mr. Ames), said, and I believe he was correct, that the manufacturers and others who are interested in the tariff would be only too glad to produce their books so as to guide the tariff makers in their work. That argument would apply equally to any proposed statistical branch in the Finance Department. I belive that the officers of such proposed statistical department could travel through the country and get information just as well as the Tariff Commission, and at much less expense. After all, if we come to examine the cost my plan would be far more economical. They might find it advisable to visit the United States. It is a very necessary thmg in framing a scientific tariff to ascertain the experience of other countries with which we are competing, both as to labour and material, and as some hon. gentlemen have said, as to transportation also; and all these things could be done by the officers of a statistical branch within the Finance Department.
Now then as to the expense. It is all very fine for hon. gentlemen opposite, with a large surplus at their credit, to say in the words of the girl ' Paw's rich, and Maw don't care.' But .there is a vast difference between the proposed Tariff Commission and a statistical branch in the Finance Department or the Customs Department. As to expense it will be a constant source of expense. The expense of the commission

itself, that is, the salaries of the three commissioners, would be unimportant in comparison with the vast expense that will be necessarily incurred in the operation of this Tariff Commission. There are secretaries and clerks belonging to the commission, with constant travelling, all of which will amount to a very large expense.
I presume, however, that that matters little to our friends on the other side of the House; we on this side of the House have always endeavoured to be economical.	,
After all the most important feature of this Bill will be the personnel of the Tariff Commission. My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) very naturally surmised and suggested *that the Tariff Commission was urged upon my hon. friends opposite by the high tariff party. We all know that there is in Canada a class of people who are in favour of a high tariff. Personally I am a moderate tariff man, I am in favour of a moderate tariff. I am in favour of a reasonable protection, but it depends entirely on what you consider a reasonable protection. I can quite imagine that a commission of this kind or a statistical committee attached to the Finance Department, if they properly attended to their duties, could gather a very great deal of information for a minister and for the government. I can quite understand they could do a great deal of good, but I can also understand that they could do a great deal of harm. Hon. gentlemen opposite who are in business know that it would be very easy for any commission to so colour their reports to the Finance Department as to get the Finance Department to increase the tariff on any particular commodity on which they wished it increased. I can see a very grave danger if the surmise of the hon. member for South Wellington is correct that this commission has been dictated by the high tariff class, that the tariff may be raised on a very plausible theory. Every business man knows that it is a simple thing for people compiling statistics to colour the statistics, and if they will only give facts, if the commission is as innocent as it actually looks, then apart from the difference in the expense it could do iust as good work as a statistical committee of the Finance Department. It would lack, however, that narticular advantage of the other system that the minister himtself would have to do a certain amount of travelling throughout the country to gain information. My hon. friends laughed at the old ministers when they compiled the tariff of 1907. Let me remind them for a moment that we sat here last year for three months and heard hon. gentlemen Mr. NESBITT.
opposite extol to high Heaven that very tariff which my hon. friend who has just sat down said was no good. We heard them extol that tariff and say they did not want any change, that the tariff was absolutely perfect.
Who said that?
All of you said that without any exception.
Will the hon. gentleman quote from ' Hansard '?

I will not bother hunting * Hansard my hon. friend knows that all of his friends said that, and said it on the platforms all over the country. First it was: Let well enough alone. Next it was: Where is it leading us, which was the same thing clothed in other words. I wish to say to my hon. friends that the tariff of 1907 compiled by the Hon. Mr. Fielding, was the best tariff ever compiled in Canada and one of the best and sanest tariffs ever compiled in the world.
My hon. friend spoke about the information which the Americans had. That information was not given by the Tariff Commission of the United States, or by the Tariff Board. Both the Tariff Board and the special Tariff Commission of the United States were appointed for the purpose of gleaning information for the Executive of the United States, and it was only last fall that any of that information was given out. It was given to the President first and only very recently, on two schedules, to the Congress of the United States. My hon. friends say they cannot change the tariff until they get the Tariff Commission appointed and get the information. Then will it not be a long time before we have any change? It has taken the Tariff Board of the United States, if I mistake not, two years to make a report on the wool and iron schedules, let .alone all the schedules that have to be gone over. My hon. friend who has just sat down told us how Bismarck sat on his throne and looked abroad across the world and saw the United States advancing more rapidly than Germany and so adopted a scientific tariff in Germany. Let me remind my hon. friends that it was only last week or the week before that they had an election in Germany and the socialists gained unprecedentedly and they are in favour of lower tariff. In the United States whichever party wins either the presidential elections or the next congressional elections, will support a lower tariff. Therefore, if there is anything in what my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) says that this Tariff Commision is simply appointed by the high tariff class in this country, there would, in my judgment, be very grave danger. I do not think we should have two classes in this country. I think the government of Can-

ada should be here to serve the interests of the whole people not od any class of the people, and I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, no matter what pressure may be brought to bear upon him, will be above catering to the views of the high tariff party and will make a tariff, whenever it is brought down, that will be just as much in the interests of the farmer and of the working man as in the interests of those who want to make fortunes in a day.
I do not know much about my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White). As I said I was pleased with the way he introduced his Bill. I, of course, know that words sometimes count for very little; some people use words to express their thoughts and others to hide them; I hope my hon. friend is not one of the latter class, and that he will carry out what he t-crld us was the intention of his party. I am strongly in favour of a department within the Finance Department and also of the ministers gathering by themselves for their own use, by contact with the people, all the information that they can gather with reference to the compiling of a tariff.
There are certain errors and anomalies no doubt in the present tariff, but that is a condition which it is impossible to avoid, because changes may take place in a business any day that would make the tariff bear hardly in some direction. But taking it as a whole, I do not think there is any man on either side of this House, who can justly say a word against the present tariff. I am sorry the Minister of Finance was not able to give us some idea of the personnel of this commission, because we could speak very much more intelligently as to the merits of the Bill if we knew from what class of the community these commissioners would be drawn. On a question of this kind you want men of ability, it is true, but you want men of more than ability, you want men of unprejudiced mind, and I need not say that there are few people in this country who have absolutely unprejudiced minds. Even the judges on the bench have to be there sometimes for a number of years before they can look at a question with an unprejudiced mind. Therefore, you want on this commission men of ability and of wideness of business knowledge, and above all, of unprejudiced views, if they are going to serve the purpose which is intended by the Minister of Finance. I would also urge on the minister that when the Bill gets into Committee of the Whole, he will reconsider his intention to appoint a permanent commission. There is no reason in the wotM why the commissioners should not stay on that board so long as they are giving service, but, on the other hand, if a commissioner be not satisfactory, there should be power
in the minister to remove him. Under the wording of the Act as at present, it would require on the part of the Minister of Finance a great deal of force of character to remove any one of these men. We are told that these commissioners are supposed to look into the cost of labour, but, surely, that ought to be the work of the Department of Labour, and if the Department of Labour is doing its duties, and has the statistics it should have, then it ought to be known what is paid for labour in every line of business throughout the country. But, there can be no particular hurry about the passage of this Bill, and I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that now, having introduced it, he should let it stand over until next session so as to allow the different Boards of Trade and other bodies throughout the country to think it over, and to formulate their opinion with regard to the proposal. So far as I am personally concerned, I think it is impossible for the Minister of Finance, or for the government, to have too much information before it in compiling a tariff, if they wish to do justice to the people of the country generally. I repeat that the Minister of Finance would have been more wisely advised had he formed a tariff bureau within his own department, and by means of which I am certain he could compile just as good a tariff as he can by utilizing the services of such a board as this.

The Minister of Finance must be highly gratified at the reception his Bill has received at the hands of the members of the House. From the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who spoke first for the opposition, to the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) who spoke last, all of them without exception have stated that so far as the Bill itself is concerned, they have little or no fault to find with it. Nearly all the arguments on the opposite side of the House have been based on the supposition of some sinister motive which they fear will be brought into the administration of this law and in regard to the appointment of the commissioners. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) made only two points in connection with the Bill, and in support of one of them he quoted the following from a speech made by the right hon. the Prime Minister:
Mv idea of a tariff is one which would give the industries of this country a fair chance and more than a fair chance perhaps, to stand up against competition in countries where it may be the standard of living among the labouring people is lower than in Canada and lower than it ought to be anywhere. That is a reasonable proposition. A permanent tariff commission if established would be

the most fitting authority to decide on this point.
Now, if there can be found anywhere a clear cut clean statement of principle in regard to the protection of all the labouring classes of this country, it is to be found in that statement, and yet we find the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) leaving out the true application of these words and endeavouring to make them apply only as between the producers and the consumers of this country. Later on, the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) said:
If they can have more than a fair chance somebody is going to suffer; it is at the expense of somebody else. At whose expense is it to be? Certainly at the expense of the great consuming masses of this country.
Now, that is a most unfair deduction from the words of the Prime Minister; no greater misstatement could be found anywhere than is to be found in that paragraph, and yet it is upon them that the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) based almost his entire argument.
The right hon. leader of the government clearly and distinctly said that in his opinion the people of Canada, in competition with nations having a lower standard of living and a lower wage scale, should have fair protection and a fair chance to build up their industries; and yet the hon. member deliberately misquoted the application of the principle so. clearly laid down. If there is one reason more than another why at this particular time I give this Bill my unqualified support, it is that hon. gentlemen opposite have played with skilled fingers on the instrument to produce discord between the various classes and portions of this Dominion. They have over and over again endeavoured to set the manufacturer against the farmer and one province against another. If there were no other reason, that reason alone would more than justify us in introducing this Bill, because when it comes to be thoroughly understood throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion that there is a commission appointed by the government of Canada, with full authority and power to act independently, to gather statistics of fact, and to collate them, not on behalf of the manufacturer, not on behalf of one class or another, but in all their relationships with each other, it will I believe do more to do away with that feeling of mistrust than any other thing that could pcssibly be conceived by this government. If there is one thing about which I have had a feeling of disgust since I became a member of this parliament, it has been this, that day after day, as we open our post office boxes, we find there special pleading for certain Bills that are asked for in this House, and that we find our corridors filled with lobbyists making special Mr. GOODEVE.
pleas on behalf of some concessions which they desire to obtain. I venture to say that if we have this independent commission appointed, it will to a very large extent check that practice, because every member of this House will have placed in his hands accurate information on which he may base his judgment. When a member on this side of the House ventured to ask the hon. member for South Wellington whether he was in favour of protection or not, his answer was: 'A tariff for revenue only.' That is not a new term in this House or throughout this country, and for a moment or two I would like to say what I conceive to be the meaning of a tariff for revenue only, and compare it with what we call a protective tariff. The principle of a tariff for revenue only is something like the principle applied at the Donnybrook fair, where-ever you see a head hit it-wherever you see a dollar, grab it. If I understand the distinction between the two parties, it is this. While both parties agree that we shall raise the revenues of this country by means of a tariff, those in favour of a tariff for revenue only are men who, disregarding all other interests, disregarding what the effect may be on the industries of the country-on the producer, the consumer, the mechanic, the labourer or the artisan-are prepared to get revenue at any cost and under any conditions, whereas those of us who are protectionists go further and say that it is our duty, in taxing the people, to see that the tariff is laid down equitably as between all classes of the community, and is so applied that every industry in the country is amply protected and nurtured in order that it may increase and grow and prosper.
If I understand it aright, that is the cardinal difference between onr friends in opposition and our friends on this side of the House. For that reason we believe that we should give careful consideration to the probable effect of every duty imposed. Knowing the intricacy of making a tariff, probably the most intricate of all the duties of a government, we believe that by gathering all the facts bearing upon the relations between the producer and the consumer, the relations between the trade of this country and the trade of foreign countries, the freight charges between the east and the west, how they apply and modify or increase the amount of protection on any particular article, we should have a thoroughly scientific tariff. The assertion made by hon. members opposite that to say we are in favour of a protective tariff means that we are in favour of an increased duty, can easily be shown to be not in accord with the facts. Over and over again the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) has shown in this House that in the actual amount of taxes taken from the people of Canada

there has been less than one per cent of difference between the so-called revenue tariff and the tariff as applied for protective purposes under the Conservative government. So that, taking the facts as they are, we find that we can give a reasonable protection that will build up our industries and develop our home markets without increasing the amount of taxes taken from the people of the Dominion. This is our reason for earnestly desiring that we should have placed in our hands all the facts hearing upon the framing of a tariff. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said: You are appointing a commission in order that you may do away with responsible government, and in order that this commission may stand between the Finance Minister -or the government and the people. I venture to say that in that, as in his other arguments, the hon. gentleman was far astray. He spent a, large portion of his time in reading extracts to show what the duties of a Royal Commission were.
Let me ask the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), what is the attitude of all railway corporations throughout the world to-day? Each of these corporations has a bureau for collecting statistical information. If you were to ask the president of any railway company on what the company is guided in its conduct of the road, he will tell you that it is largely guided by the facts furnished by its statistical bureau. Surely no one in this House will venture to say that the staffs of these bureaus of statistics appointed to collect the facts, are the men who are really managing and regulating the policies of these railway companies.
Another argument advanced is that by the appointment of this commission, we are doing away with constitutional government, and making these Tariff Commis-missioners the real framers of the tariff. Let me give another illustration to show the fallacy of that argument. I had the privilege of listening the other evening to Sir Edmond Byron Walker when he gave a sketch of the operations of the large financial institution of which he is the head. After he had placed before his hearers very clearly some salient facts in connection with the progress of that institution, he said:
If there is any gentleman present who at any time, when any trade question arises, would like to avail himself of the information possessed by our bureau of statistical information he is welcome to it. By simply sending word we will be pleased to place at his disposal all the facts connected with trade questions.
What was the important point brought out by that statement of Sir Edmond Walker, who is at the head of one of the 86
largest financial institutions in Canada? Sir Edmond realized that no institution could act promptly or formulate any policy with regard to trade unless the facts were in its possession, and he ventured to say that the Bank of Commerce had at its* disposition one of the best means of ascertaining all facts in connection with trade and commerce that could be found in the Dominion, but would anybody venture to say that because these banking institutions have each a bureau for gathering statistical facts to enable them to better administer the funds entrusted to their care, the directors were delegating to the men they appointed to collect those statistics the management of these institutions? 1 do not think any hon. member would have the hardihood to make any assertion of the kind, but hon. gentlemen opposite do not hesitate to take that ground when it enables them to criticise a policy of the government. All that these Tariff Commissioners will be appointed to do is merely to collect and collate all the facts in connection with the various industries of this country. They_ will then place these facts before the minister, who in turn will submit them to the government and the House. There is a clause providing that, under certain conditions, the members of the commission may withhold secret confidential information obtained by them in the course of their investigation. ' Every hon. member will realize the necessity of a provision of that kind. Hon. members will see the necessity of reporting the facts to the minister who administers the revenues of this country, and who will use his discretion and judgment in giving these facts to the House. In my opinion this Bill is a step taken in advance legislation, and I am glad that the government have had the courage to implement the promise made in this connection by the right hon. the First Minister. The bringing down by him of this Bill will be a great factor in restoring business confidence throughout all portions of this Dominion.
In the late campaign, I was able, owing to the very unusual and peculiar circumstances to give a unique illustration of how this tariff will work out under certain conditions. It was largely owing to these peculiar iconditions that I gained the great majority which I did in the last election.
