When you left the Chair at six o'clock I had just given an illustration of one of the effects of the tariff, and was showing how it was inter-related to so many other industries in the province of British Columbia. I will not attempt to work out in detail the result of the tariff on that particular industry, as my object was simply to make .an illustration of the necessity of a commission of this kind in order to ascertain all the facts, and bring them before the House and the people. We have another great industry in our province, namely, zinc and lead. This is probably one of the most technical and complicated of the natural resources we have in the Dominion. They are a class of metals that are difficult to handle, and yet are used in nearly every industry in Canada. We had a clear illustration of that principle a number of years ago, when all the Boards of Trade in the Dominion of Canada met in the provincial House in the city of Toronto, with the president of the Toronto Board of Trade in the chair. At that time we were seeking in British Columbia to obtain a readjustment of the old tariff, and it was pointed out how the whole industry of the manufacture of agricultural implements would be affected by any change in that particular tariff. But the result of our getting together and frankly discussing the entire situation in all its bearings, was that we were able to induce the government to make some slight alteration in the tariff, with the result that there was established in the city of Montreal a large corroding work in which a large amount of capital is invested, and which has been a great employer of labour. Here is one of the natural resources of an outlying province, away out on the Pacific coast, and yet it directly and indirectly affects a great industry in the largest commercial city in the Dominion of Canada. There again is an illustration of the necessity for actual information in regard to these matters which concern the tariff.

Then we have another great natural resource in that province, one that has been recently discussed in this House, I refer to (the great lumber industry, the one in which probably more capital is invested than in any other industry in our province, and one which is vital to the prosperity and growth of our province. Now I think every hon. member will admit there has been an effort made by nearly every hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House to try and set the farmer against any protection of that great industry in our province. It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the relation of that industry to the Bill before the House; I merely want to say that every lumberman in the province of British Columbia, yes, every lumberman throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion from Nova Scotia westward, would welcome a thorough investigation into their business, and I believe it could be shown, and would be shown, that it is not only in the interest of this great industry itself, but in the interest as well of the farmers and of all other people in this Dominion, that that industry should receive protection. So along these broader lines, not in any narrow way, but in the very broadest way, we believe this Bill is a great step in the right direction, because we think it will engender a confidence in the minds of all classes of the community. We believe in no other way could the same confidence be engendered in the minds of the people as by the appointment of this independent commission, which would be free from the control of parliament, and would be just as independent as the Railway Commission, which has won the confidence of the people of Canada. It is because I believe also, Mr. Speaker, that it will bring the consumer and the producer together and will thus be in the interest of the worker and the labouring man as well as the manufacturer, that I am strongly in favour of this Bill. I want to say that I have absolutely no sympathy with the little provincials, men whose vision is bounded by the gate posts of their front yard and the pumphandle in their back yard, men who would cut and carve this great Dominion into small sections, divided by schisms, men whose souls are shrunken by the dollars that they wotild tie around them. We take a broader view of the destiny of this great country. Indeed it is difficult for us to grasp the great future of this wondrous Dominion of ours. In 1 addition to the music caused by the rustling of the golden grain on our wind swept prairies, in addition to the lowing of the kine and the bleating of the sheep on its foothills, we should yet see great factories established in our western districts, making use of our inexhaustible supplies of coal and iron, and yet cheaper raw ma-861
terials of natural gas and electrical energies of our great water-powers, giving employment to an ever increasing population in varied industries. I call the attention of this House to the fact that there lies in our great west, not only the magnificent coal-bearing strata to which I have referred, but the very cheapest power known in the civilized world to day. We have this great glacier bed producing electricity in abundance, we have natural gas in abundance, we have the iron, we have the coal, we have everything that goes to form the basic necessities for a wonderful manufacturing development. On that ground I appeal to this House, to both sides of this House, in support of this Bill. We should not treat this as a political matter, we should seek the best way of developing every portion of this far-flung empire. On that ground, believing as I do not only in interprovincial, inter-dominion and inter-imperial trade, believing as I do that in working together along the lines outlined by this Bill, we can build up in this great Dominion the brightest gem in the greatest commercial empire the world has ever seen, I shall have much pleasure in supporting this Bill.

Bi. CARVELL (Carleton, New Brunswick). I do not know whether I would come within the class of the narrow, contracted back yard politicians that my hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) has been so graphically describing, or whether I would be one of the empire builders that he has spoken of in the latter part of his peroration. But, Sir, unfortunately perhaps for myself, I am unable to arrive at the same conclusion as the hon. gentleman in regard to the value or necessity of this Bill. I think that no person can find fault with the government for attempting to get information on every question which enters into Die lives of the Canadian people; and if I believed that this Bill was only for the purpose ^ of getting accurate information on all the great trade questions, I could not find very much fault with it. I am bound to assume that the Minister of Finance is sincere when he tells us that he wants to get information. Perhaps it would not be derogatory to the hon. gentleman-I am sorry he is not in the House at this moment-to tell him that he has not been in public life very long; he does not know the wiles of the deceptive politician, and until we have some evidence to the contrary, it is only fair to say that he is sincere in trying to get the information.
Let us look for a moment at the origin and history of the scheme which has resulted in bringing down this Bill. We had not any difficulty when our friends were in power in getting information on which to frame a Tariff Bill. In 1897 and in 1907 the ministers of the Crown made an itiner-

ary over the Dominion of Canada. They gathered a lot of information, they codified that information, and on that information they framed a Tariff Bill. I remember distinctly that instead of finding fault with these gentlemen for getting the information, fault was found that they were spending too much time over it. But let that be as it will, the late government were able to frame a tariff under which Canada prospered more in the next ten years than she had ever done in all her previous history. If conditions had remained as favourable as they were during those ten years, then I cannot say that there would have been much need of a change. But conditions change in Canada as well as in all other parts of the world, and the time came when the government found it necessary, in the course of eight or ten years more, to make another itinerary of Canada to see what the changed conditions were. Messrs. Fielding and Paterson, with a very able secretary, whom I am sorry to say is not now in the employ of tiie government, travelled from one end of this country to the other, they obtained further information, and on this further and additional information they framed the Tariff Act of 1907. There were not many changes made, perhaps not as many changes as some of us would have liked to see made; but I maintain that the viciousness which has sprung from the tariff had not commenced to show itself in 1900 or in 1907 as it does at the present day. Therefore, as there are changed conditions, we need a change in the tariff.
It is in the mind of every hon. member in this House, of every thinking man in Canada, that the time has come when there will be a change in our tariff relations. It has been argued here that all over the world where the highest tariffs prevail we have had the greatest prosperity and three-quarters of the speakers on the other side of the House have instanced Germany and the United States,as evidence of the greatest prosperity and have ascribed that prosperity to a high protective tariff. If that be true, it is a remarkable thing that in all of these countries a very serious agitation is going on to get a reduction of these high protective tariffs. I spent a few days in Germany last summer and although I was not able to make as extensive economic investigations as I would like, every man I was able to talk with, and I am sorry their number was not large, claimed that the taxation was something terrific, the cost of living almost beyond endurance and what with the taxation and the army and navy they could not tell what was going to happen. It was prophesied to me by many people that the result of the next election would show a wonderful increase in the representation of the Socialists, and Mr. CARVELL.
the elections have shown this prophecy to have been well founded. We know that the doctrine of the Socialists is not only to get rid of the army and navy expenditure, but to get rid of high protection as well, because high protection in Germany is producing to a very great extent the same results as it is producing in the United States and in Canada.
I come now to the greatest example of high protection the world has seen, the United States. I do not think my hon. friends the high protectionists of Canada will claim that the great development _ in the United States is altogether due to high protection. The United States would have developed in the last 50 years if they had not had a tariff at all. The very richness of their soil, the prodigality of their natural products, the great influx of population from all over the world, naturally make the United States great. The United States would have become a great country without a tariff. If they had resorted to direct-taxation, they would have had an enormous prosperity, but they would not have had the conditions that they have to-day, the trusts, mergers and combines, with which they are now contending. The result of this high protection has been to create these trusts, mergers and combines, and now we have a revulsion of feeling, almost amounting to a revolution in the United States against the condition of affairs which the tariff has created. A year and a half ago when elections were held over a great portion of the United States, the high protection party was swept out of power from end to end of that country. It is hard to tell what may take place in the next elections owing to conflicting interests, all we have to do is to read the papers and there we will see that there is the same unrest in the United States to-day as there was two years ago and I do not think a person can be blamed for prophesying that no matter which party may come into power as the result of the next election there will be a reduction of tariffs and the voice of the people will be a protest against the high taxation under which they are groaning now. Take any newspaper in the United States, take the Boards of Trade, take any expression of public opinion and there you will find ^ simply pne outcry against the enormous* cost of living.
Coming to the Dominion of Canada, w'e find exactly the same condition of affairs, we find the same outcry going up from the people against the high cost of living. Who are better able to judge the political and the public barometer than our protectionist friends or the Manufacturers' Association? We find that away back in 1909 the Manufacturers' Association at their annual conference first intimated or proposed this idea of a Tariff Commission

and a resolution was passed at that meeting embodying this do-ctrine and suggesting that the government should appoint such a commission. We heard very little about that Tariff Commission for the next year or two. It is true that just before the election the right hon. the leader of this House (Mr. Borden) advocated it as a plank in his platform. But let me show you what was the attitude of the gentlemen who were the originators and the fathers of this scheme, who have urged it along and who will benefit by it. When you learn the views of these gentlemen you will not have much difficulty in arriving at a conclusion as to who is behind this scheme and whom it will benefit and what the result and general scope of the investigations of this commission will be.
I find that at the meeting of the Manufacturers' Association held in Toronto in October last this matter was referred to by practically every speaker who discussed tariff questions. I have no quarrel with the Manufacturers' Association as individual members of the community. They are gentlemen who are working in their own interests and when working in their own interests they probably believe they are working in the interests of Canada. They are controlling large industries, they are doing a great work for Canada, and I do not wish to say anything derogatory to the individual members. I do, however, say and I think I shall not be contradicted that the one aim and object of the Manufacturers' Association as an association is to secure as much protection as they possibly can for their manufactured products and to obtain their raw materials free of duty, wherever it is possible to do so. That I take as being the aim and object of the Manufacturers' Association of Canada. This matter was referred to by President Rowley in his address. He concludes that address as follows:
No matter what the cost may be, and no matter whose toes may be trodden upon, let us first get our tariff right and fair-
That is right and fair from the manufacturers' standpoint.
-then let us ensure its stability, making from time to time only such slight modifications as the changed conditions of the country demand. As manufacturers we should be able, we should .be willing to view the creation of a Tariff Commission with complacency; so I hope we will all facilitate this work as far as we can, by giving such data as we are able to snpply.
You do not find any protest on the part of the Manufacturers' Association. The president says: Let us get our tariff right and fair and as manufacturers we can view the workings of this commission with complacency. But that is mild compared with statements made by the chairman of the Tariff Branch of the commission, Mr. Russell, of the Russell Motor Car Company of Toronto. Mr. Russell makes a very exhaustive report on practically every branch of the Canadian manufacturing industries, and when he comes to .this particular branch he makes some remarks which I think are of more than ordinary importance when we consider the manner in which certain gentlemen on the other side of the House have received the suggestions or perhaps stronger terms which we have used against this Bill. The right hon. leader himself, I thought with more heat than was really necessary or perhaps entirely proper in view of the splendid work which the Manufacturers' Association did for him in September last, took particular pains to disavow any connection with the Manufacturers' Association and even went so far as to say that only one member of that association had ever spoken to him about it and that member was opposed to it.
Well, we have to take the word of the right hon. gentleman, but I would like to know if the Minister of Finance would pledge his_ word to the same extent and I would like to know if the Minister of Trade and Commerce would make the same declaration as the Prime Minister has made. Does the Conservative party expect the people to believe that the Manufacturers' Association are not the originators of this scheme? Are not the men who are behind the Manufacturers' Association the men who are pushing this legislation along and are they not the men who will benefit by it? Why, you only have to take the history of the Conservative party since 1878, and the question is answered. The Manufacturers' Association and the high protectionists are the men who want this legislation and it is to pay them for their magnificent support in September last, and to carry out the principle advocated by them in all these years that'this Bill is being promulgated. I make bold to say that on account of that very thing, more than anything else, I am opposed to this Bill. The Minister of Finance told us, and the supporters of the government have reiterated the statement, that it was never intended that the commission would have anything to do with making laws, and that the information they collect will be handed to the government and the government will frame the tariff as the government sees fit. That is true, taking the literal wording of the Bill, but what are the views of Mr. Russell, Chairman of the Tariff Branch of the Manufacturers' Association? I quote from 'Industrial Canada' for November, 1911, the words of Mr. Russell:
Usually commissions which have been appointed have been appointed for administra-

live work, for carrying out administration. This commission lias to do an entirely different thing. It has to do no administration work but law-making work, the actual making of the laws; the making of the laws for which the parliament of Canada will be responsible. The composition of that Tariff Commission and its ability to obtain information, the use which will be made of that information, whether public or private, and all that sort of thing is going to he of tremendous importance to the whole of Canada and to the manufacturng interests perhaps specially, and I think it is of tremendous importance that our tariff committee for this coming year shall be seized with the importance of that and prepare their recommendations accordingly.
Well, Sir, -when you read that statement of the chairman of the Tariff Branch of the Manufacturers' Association, you have the whole thing in a nutshell; you have the very thing that the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) contended for; you have the very thing for which the Liberal party of Canada is contending today, and you have the pith of the reasons why we are asked to pass this legislation. Does anyone mean to tell me that- the government are going to appoint a commission which will cost from $50,000 to $100,000 a year and keep this commission doing nothing else but investigating? Remember that this commission is only going to make such investigation as the Minister of Finance requires them to make and that when the Minister of Finance asks this commission to make an investigation into the cost of production of any article in Canada and they submit a report of their findings, does any man mean to tell me that the government will not accept the findings of that commission in framing their tariff? Why did the government appoint this commission, why did the government give this commission such powers, why spend all this money on it if they do not accept their recommendation? No matter how you work it out, indirectly this commission is to make the tariff law of Canada.

Will the hon. gentleman show me any clause in the Bill which authorizes the commission to recommend any particular line of action?
, Mr. CARVELL. I am surprised that my hon. friend asked me that question. I tell my hon. friend that section 4 of this Bill provides what are the duties of the commission and the hon. gentleman cannot show me where that commission has power to make one bit of investigation except under the direction and at the instigation of the Minister of Finance.

My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell), has not answered my question. The hon. gentleman said that if this commission made a recommendation the government would be bound to follow it, and Mr. CARVELL.
I say there is no clause in the Bill which provides for any such thing.

I do not think my hon. friend does his intelligence the justice which it demands. In the first place I never said so. I said that' no man could conceive of a government going to all that expense, and all this trouble unless they were to accept the findings of this commission, and I repeat it. And my hon. friend knows, and I repeat it, that they have no power to investigate anything except what they are directed to investigate by the Minister of Finance, or by the government, and my hon. friend knows they will make no investigation into anything only what they are told to investigate. I go further and I say that my hon. friend ought to know that they will only investigate that which the government wants them to investigate, and if the government wants to put a duty on a certain article they will send the commission after it, and they will be pretty liable to get the evidence which, in their opinion, will justify them in raising the duty. I believe this Bill should not be adopted because it is misleading; it will not produce the results expected of it in the way of taking evidence. The whole object of this Bill and the only powers conferred on the commission under this Bill are to investigate into cost, price, transportation, labour, &c., when so directed by the minister. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), spoke last night on this question, and he is a gentleman whose honesty when discussing tariff matters I always admire. The hon. member (Mr. Ames) told the whole story. He said that these gentlemen need not necessarily be Conservatives in order to have a place on this commission, but he said they must be high protectionists.
I beg your pardon; the words ' high protectionists ' were not used by me. I said they must be in sympathy with the well known sentiment of the present government.
My hon. friend will not quarrel with me very much when I say that that means that they must be protectionists.
Yes, but I did not say anything about high protectionists.

My hon. friend (Mr. Ames), said they are going to appoint a commission of protectionists, and he says this commission will not have any trouble in getting evidence, because, he says: ' we will furnish the evidence.' Well, that is just what we object to. When the minister sends out the commission to investigate the cost of boots and .shoes, of course 1 we '

will furnish the evidence, and 'we' will take mighty good pains to see that no evidence gets before the commission except the evidence which justifies either a retention of the present duties or an increase as high as my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) can get it. That is the kind of evidence that this commission will get, and that is one reason why I object to it. I object to it again, because of the secret clauses in it. I do not believe the present parliament has any right to pry into a man's private affairs. The result of this will be that nine-tenths of the evidence which is adduced before this commission-because remember the only evidence we will have in the ordinary working out of it will be the evidence of the manufacturers themselves-will be evidence which the protectionists and the protectionists commission will consider as confidential, and therefore the public will not be allowed to have it.
The result will be that we shall have findings by this commission, but we shall not have the evidence on which those findings are baised. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), last evening said that we on this side of the House should welcome this commission as a means of getting information, but in the working out of this scheme, we shall have very little information. There will be confidential information given to the commission, but we shall have only the conclusions of the commission without seeing the information on which its conclusions have been reached. There has been considerable talk here about the necessity for information. I do not think anybody denies the necessity for information, but I do not believe there is much necessity for more information than we have at the present time. Hon, gentlemen opposite talk about this haphazard tariff; but this haphazard tariff has got along pretty well so far as Canada is concerned, and the people of Canada have got along pretty well under that tariff. If you went to-day to the Departments of Trade and Commerce, Finance and' Customs, I believe that you would get pretty nearly as much information as you would require in order to come to a pretty good conclusion as to what is necessary in framing a tariff for any branch of Canadian industry. I wonder if the hon. member for St. Antoine thinks that it is necessary to appoint a Tariff Commission to tell the government 'whether the duty of 30 per cent on boots and shoes should be retained in the interest of this country, or raised' to 35 or 40 per cent, when the fact is known to every man who thinks in Canada that the hides from which leather for those boots and shoes is made comes into this country free of duty. We had the admission of the hon. member for St. Antoine in this House the other evening that with
a preference of only 5 per cent the Canadian manufacturers of boots and shoes could wrest the trade of Australia away from the United States; and then, he tells us that we cannot make boots and shoes in Canada to compete with those from the United States without 30 per cent protection. Does he think the government wants further information on that point? If they ask the hon. member for St. Antoine, they will get all the information they want.

Is the hon. gentleman aware that the boot 'and shoe manufacturers of Canada were never abie to persuade the Conservative government that they needed over 25 per cent protection, but that -the Liberal government gave them 30 per cent without their asking for it?

I was not a member of that government, and, therefore, I cannot answer my hon. friend's question; but I can hardly believe it-I do not say that offensively. If the hon. gentleman wants us to believe that the boot and shoe manufacturers of Canada never asked for more protection during the days of the Conservative government, they were a different class of people from the men who are manufacturing boots and shoes in Canada to-day. Now, my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) this afternoon stated that he was not a high protectionist, but a low protectionist. Well, I have always a great deal of confidence in anything which that hon. gentleman says, because in my judgment he is one of the ablest men and possesses one of the best reasoning minds in this House. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie does not require information from a Tariff Commission to show him that the time has come when the duty on farm machinery should be reduced, because last year he introduced a resolution into this House, and spoke upon it on more than one occasion, declaring that the time had come when the duty on agricultural implements should be reduced. Do the other hon. gentlemen from western Canada want any further evidence? The manufacturers of farm machinery in Canada last year not only supplied two-thirds or more of the home market, but exported between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000 of farm machinery to all the civilized countries of the globe, in competition with the whole world. In the face of that fact, do these hon. gentlemen want any further evidence from an expert Tariff Commission to enable them to decide whether the duty on farm machinery should be retained at 174 per cent, or reduced ? I will tell you in what respect I think the evidence of an expert Tariff Commission will be useful to our hon. friends opposite. The primary

object of this measure is, I believe, to get at just such wavering minds as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and other members from the western portion of this Dominion. In 1907 thirteen hon. members supporting the Conservative party did not want any further evidence to convince them that the time had arrived when the duty should be taken off agricultural implements, and I see two or three of those gentlemen before me tonight. So firmly were they convinced of the necessity of that demand that on the third reading of the Tariff Bill they moved an amendment, and compelled their own leader to vote against it, in order to put themselves on record; and these men have gone through western Canada from that day to this parading the fact that they had voted for the reduction or abolition of the duty on farm machinery. These hon. gentlemen did not want any further evidence in 1907; the hon. member for Portage la Prairie did not want any further evidence last year; but the government wiants further evidence, because the government wants to show these men that they are wrong-^and see how simple it is. The government appoints this commission; it hands over to it a certain statement; it says we want you to investigate the question of the duty on farm machinery, and give us the evidence that will convince the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that he is wrong; and in all probability they will produce the evidence. That is one of the reasons I am opposing this Bill. But it may be said that I am imputing bad faith, that I am drawing conclusions not warranted by the facts. I say I am not.
That is the logical conclusion of this Bill which is forced upon the government by the Manufacturers' Association. It is the logical conclusion of this Bill which only gives the commissioners the right to get information when directed to do so by the Finance Minister. It is the logical conclusion of a Bill which only enables the tariff commissioners to get the sort of information the Finance Minister may require. It these commissioners were at liberty to gather information at their own discretion and of their own free will, without dictation from anybody, one of the great objections to this measure would be removed. But if they had such power, that would defeat the very purpose of this legislation, because we might get a man on that commission who would have sufficient industry to do some work on his own initiative and who would summon before the commission parties who would not give the kind of evidence which the government required. Therefore the government have taken precaution to muzzle their own ap-Mr. CARVELL.
pointees so that they will not be able to do anything except what they are directed to do.
Do the government want information from an expert tariff commission to tell them whether it is necessary to grant a bounty to the manufacturers of iron _in this country, after these manufacturers have received some $15,000,000 in bounties in the last 15 or 18 years? Surely not. Do the people of this country believe that the iron and steel industry needs a bounty? I am not going to talk bounties now because we shall probably have an opportunity later on to discuss them.
What does your hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) say?

I have no care for the opinions of any man on earth on this question. I am giving my own. Let me tell you, Sir, that when the Dominion Iron people were trying to get the bounties renewed last year, their great plea was that by the reciprocity agreement they were going to lose eight cents per ton on coal and therefore ought to be recouped by a duty on steel rods. Well, the duty on coal was not removed, yet they are coming here asking the government to make them a present of a half a million or a million dollars more in the shape of a bounty. Do my friends from western Canada, who are not directly interested in the manufacture of iron and steel, want any evidence to convince them that- a bounty is unnecessary? I should say not.
I come to another item. I think it was the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) who wanted evidence regarding the cement industry. I am surprised that there should be a man in Canada who wants further evidence in order to come to a conclusion as to whether or not the duty should be retained on cement, after the evidence given by Sir Sanford Fleming during the last eight or nine months. Sir Sanford Fleming gave evidence which was incontrovertible. He proved that some shrewd capitalists bought up practically all the cement industries in the country for $12,000,000, merged them into a combine, issued $7,000,000 of bonds, and $10,000,000 of preferred stock, and placed that stock on the market at par. They paid for the property and had $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 to the good, then they issued $13,000,000 of common stock, which is now selling at 28 cents on the dollar.
How much did the Liberal party propose to reduce that duty by the reciprocity agreement?
Eight cents per barrel.
How does that compare with the duty imposed by the United States?	.
It brings it to about the same.
I beg your pardon, it did not.

If that came from any other hon. gentleman, I would ask your ruling Mr. Speaker, but as I do not care what the hon. member for Frontenac may say, I shall not ask him to withdraw it.
But hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that they want further evidence on the question of cement.
Does it not, I would ask, appeal to the intelligence of every one, that when you can bring cement from England, Germany or Belgium and lay it down at any Canadian seaport or lake port at 50 cents per barrel cheaper than you can buy it from the manufacturing industry in Canada, and when you can go to any of the American lake ports and buy cement there 50 cents cheaper than you can in Canada, and when you have in the freight from the seaboard or lakeport all the protection that you can need-is it necessary to have a Tariff Commission to tell us whether the duty ought to be retained on cement or not? That is about as preposterous as the argument of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) about the duty on boots and shoes.	_
Another objection I have to this Bill, which is as vital as any of the others I have enumerated, is that it does not provide for any investigation into the capital stock of any of those companies engaged in manufacturing. Take the cement industry as an example. Let us suppose that this Tariff Commission is going to investigate the cement industry. They will go to the cement combine and ask how much it costs to make a barrel of cement. They will ask that combine to produce its books and we will suppose that the combine gives correct answers. Let us suppose that the combine gives correct information and full information regarding the cost of transportation and the other expenses that enter into the cost of production, the commission will then be met by this plea on behalf of the cement company :	You have no right to reduces the
duty because if you do we shall not be able to pay dividends. We have to pay interest on the bonds, dividends on the preferred stock, and we ought to pay dividends on the common stock. But if you reduce the duty, we shall not be able to pay dividends on the preferred stock much less on the common stock; and the Tariff Commission will report that it would be an injustice to reduce the duty on cement. But, there is one thing, on which the commission will have no evidence whatever and on which they will not have the power to obtain evidence, and that is as to the amount of water in the capital stock.
They will not be able to determine whether the $13,000,000 common stock is all water, besides $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 of preferred stock. The result will be that this commission will submit a report to the government, not based on the real facts at all. I would be glad if any hon. member will show me where, in the four corners of this Bill, this commission has the power to inquire into the capitalization of any company and ascertain how much is cash, and how much water and on what amount of capital the company ought to pay dividends. Without that power the commissioners might as well be kicking their heels around Sparks Street as trying to investigate any combine.
For these reasons I am opposed to this Bill. The only possible excuse for it is to furnish the government with some pretext for making the protective features of the tariff still more protective.
There cannot be any other reason for it. I oppose it because this body has not sufficient investigating power; it has no initiative. These commissioners can only investigate what they are told to investigate, and have no power to institute investigations of their own and learn the conditions of any branch of trade except those which they are directed to investigate. Their conclusions must of necessity be incomplete and inefficient, and must be an unsafe basis for action by the government. Above all things I oppose this measure because, in my opinion, no matter what may be the avowed intention, the logical result, the necessary, the only logical result, will be to foist upon the people of Canada a higher protection than that under which we are groaning at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I had always lassumed that Don Quixote was the fantastical creation of a vivid imagination, nothing real about him, there may, perhaps be some allegory in it. Had the author lived now, he might have applied his idea of Don Quixote to hon. gentlemen opposite. They have raised in their imaginations ghosts, spectres and bugaboos in respect of this Bill, .and, having raised them, they are prepared to' overthrow them. It is stated of Don Quixote that on one occasion when he was riding with Sancho Panza and looked out upon the plains, and saw aibout thirty substantial windmills, he said to his companion, ' Providence directs our efforts better than we ourselves could have wished. Look yonder, friend Sancho P-anza; there are at least thirty outrageous giants whom I intend to encounter, and, having deprived them of life we will enrich ourselves with the spoils, for they are our lawful prize and the extirpation of that cursed brood will be an ac-
Never breathless.

No, never breathless, I take the expression back and apologize to hon. gentlemen opposite. They are never breathless. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have told hon. gentlemen on the other side that, the purpose of the Bill is to ascertain the fact of the cost of production of commodities at home and abroad, and other facts. The hon. member who has just spoken, says that the inquiry is to be limited, and that the commissioners cannot inquire into such things as the

capitalization of the companies. If the hon. gentlemen will look at the last two
Clauses of section 

 of the Bill, he will find the fallowing :
All conditions and factors which affect and enter into the cost of production and the price to the consumer in Canada.
What does that include? It includes the amount of capital
No, the cost of production, not the capitalization.
I presume that the capitalization of the company, the capital invested in it, will be a factor in determining the cost of production.
So do I.

Book further, and you find this provision:
Generally all the conditions affecting production, manufacture, cost and price in Canada as compared with other countries.
We have been told by the right hon. the Premier and the Minister of Finance, that, in order to ascertain the facts broadminded, virile men will be appointed, men capable and -experienced in investigations, men capable of ascertaining facts, analysing, and systematizing them, report them to the government and the House, and the House will give them to the people. For nothing will satisfy the people except full information. The safety of democratic legislation lies in publicity. So the hon. minister has said frankly that what is aimed at is to ascertain the facts and he will submit the facts to the government, the House, and the people. It is objected that the Bill says the commissioners are also to submit their ' results.' ' Who sticks in the letter sticks in the bark.' And what are their results? Simply the facts they have ascertained. .Nowhere in the Bill is it stated that the board to be appointed is to submit its opinion and recommendations and suggestions to the minister, to the government, or to the House, and upon the facts so ascertained and reported is to be based a tariff which is to -govern the trade of Canada. A tariff is essential iand necessary. For the country is committed to the principle of protection.
We must have a protective tariff. I am well aware that some years ago hon. gentlemen opposite and their predecessors did not have that idea. For instance, at the Liberal convention in 1893 we find the Hon. Wilfrid Laurier saying:
But I appeal to your judgment in the face of the experience of the last fifteen years under the system which was introduced toy the Conservative government which was dubbed the National Policy to say if -that system is not vicious in principle, iniquitous in

its terms and dangerous in its consequences. I say that it is vicious in principle. I want to know-and I put the question so as to be heard through the length and breadth of this country-by virtue of what principle will you tax a man to enrich his neighbour? By virtue of what principle will you tax the farmer in order to give work to the workingman? On what principle will you tax the workingman in order to give better prices to the farmer?
A little further on he stated:
I submit to you that the ideal fiscal system is the British system of free trade. Sir, my loyalty, as I have stated, does not ooze from the pores of my body, but I do want to go for an example to the mother country, aDd not to the United States, much as I respect and love the people on the other side of the line. I say the policy should be a policy of free trade, such as they have in England, but I am sorry to say that the circumstances of the country cannot admit, at present, of that policy in its entirety. But I do propose to you that from this day henceforward it should be the goal to which we aspire.
Three years after that the right hon. gentleman and his party attained power, and what happened then? Did they adopt free trade as it was in England? They adopted the policy that was dubbed the National Policy, and the country has lived under that policy to the present day. It is true that the right hon. leader of the opposition and his friends recently *endeavoured to depart from that policy, and they have been corrected for it. So we may take it as ia fact that the settled policy of Canada is a policy of protection. As other young nations have prospered under such a policy, as Germany and the United States have prospered under it, so is Canada prospering under it. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Carvell) has declared that Canada is prosperous. Why? Because of the protective policy. Now if a protective policy is right, and we believe it is right, we must see to it that the protection is a reasonable one. I believe that every supporter of the government in this House is in favour of a reasonable policy of protection. They do not want a high protection, but they want some measure of protection, and if it is necessary to have a tariff it (must be a sane tariff. In order to have a sane tariff it is necessary to know the facts. I think I may state it as a principle that a protective tariff that will be justified by the country must be one which, in respect to the various commodities which are produced in Canada, either largely or entirely from our own raw material, will be based on the cost of the production of the article imported, the cost of its transportation to Canada plus the duty, equalling the cost of production in Canada plus a reasonable profit to manufacturers.
Now what	does such a principle
involve? It involves the necessity of an inquiry into the cost of production at home and abroad, the necessity of an inquiry	into the transportation rates,
into the capitalization of great companies, into the cost of labour, and all other things which go to make up the equation I have mentioned.
If that be necessary, we must have capable men and experienced men to make that inquiry. It has been suggested by an hon. member on tlhe other side that it was the duty of the Finance Minister to visit the factories and industrial centres, and find out for himself how matters stand. Imagine a minister visiting all those factories to find out what was going on; imagine him attending all the labour congresses, all the farmers' conventions, in order to ascertain their wishes and their views. What would happen in his department while he was gone? Already the ministers of this government have too much work on their hands, so much that it is impossible for them to look after the details of their offices; and yet this hon. gentleman proposes to throw upon their shoulders the additional duty of visiting all the manufacturing establishments in this country. I think the true solution of this question lies in the establishment of the commission that is proposed by this Bill. It will be necessary for the government to ascertain the facts in order that they may formulate a policy based thereon. It will not do for the farmer to say that he must be protected to the detriment of his fellow citizens, or for the labourer to say that he must be protected to the exclusion of all others, or for the manufacturer to say the same thing; This Tariff Commission must ascertain just what facts are causing the contention of each class. If the tariff is to be so arranged that important object which should claim the 'attention of this 'Commission, that the cost of the production of the article in the foreign country, with the cost of transportation to Canada plus the duty, is to equal the cost of production in Canada plus a reasonable profit to the producer, if then that point is departed from downwards, the result will be that the Canadian producer will lose the Canadian market, the labouring man will lose an opportunity for employment in Canada at fair wagfes and the manufacturer will have to go out of business. On the other hand, if the tariff is raised beyond that point, there will shortly arise what the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) described as informal trusts and combines, which are things not to be desired. The hon. gentleman said that they had already arisen. Perhaps they have, but why have they arisen? Because the tariff has not been properly adjusted, because it is not

correct in principle. If they have arisen they have arisen under the administration of the late government. But a proper tariff will correct those evils, will prevent the origination of combines. Therefore, I say it is very desirable that the government should ascertain all the facts, obtain all the information possible, on which to base a sane tariff, and such a tariff will undoubtedly correct the irregularities 'and discrepancies wihicih are now complained of. We are hearing complaints from the farmers of this country, we are hearing complaints from the western farmers that the tariff bears unequally upon them, and I am inclined to think that it does. But I am pleased to have the assurance of some members of the government that one of the first things that will he done by the Tariff Commission will be to ascertain the facts concerning the condition of the agriculturists in Canada. If that is done, I feel confident that better conditions may toe brought about for 'the farmer, that the interests of the employed will toe conserv.ed without prejudice to the employer, that the interests of the manufacturer will toe safeguarded without -any detriment to the workingman or the farmer. Ail these various interests must be considered in order to frame a tariff that will bear equally upon all! classes of our population. If a proper tariff is obtained protecting properly the farmer, the industrial labourer and the manufacturer our country will prosper and many people will not have to resort as they did before 1879 to the soup kitchen for their existence.

I wish to direct the attention of the hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) to page 2495 of 'Hansard', January, 1911, which contained the speech of Hon. Mr. Fielding with regard to this reciprocity agreement. I asked the hon. member: How much did the Liberal party propose to reduce the duty on cement by the reciprocity agreement? His answer was, 8 cents. I said next: How7 did that compare with the duty on cement imposed by the United States government? His answer was it made it equal. I said no, it did not.
Under the reciprocity agreement I want to refer the hon. member to the page already quoted where the minister says that under the reciprocity agreement the United States tariff will be 8 cents. The rate proposed by Canada will be 11 cents. The reduction proposed by Canada was 1J cents. I ask the hon. gentleman to take that into consideration along with his statements in. answer to my questions a while ago and see if he feels justified in the heat he displayed and the rather discourteous manner in which he referred to myself.
My hon. friend asked about coal, and I said 8 cents.
I was not talking about coal, I w7as talking about cement.
I was talking about coal, he asked the American rate, and I said it was the same, that it would bring it to the same.
' Hansard ' to-morrow will show your position to be even more ridiculous than ever. 1

I heard the question put by the hon. member for Frontenac .(Mr. Edwards), and I am positive that the question could only have related to the proposed reduction of the duty on coal, under the proposed reciprocity agreement.
Oh, oh.
It does not do to say oh, oh. The hon. member w7as talking about coal when the hon. member for Frontenac put the question.
I was talking about coal.

It was not my intention to take any part in this debate, but after some of the view's which have been expressed with reference to this Bill for the appointment of a Tariff Commission, I feel I w'ould not he doing my duty to myself or to my constituents if I did not discuss for a few moments some of these questions. I was not surprised to hear the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) advocating the appointment of a Tariff Comission, or advocating a protective tariff in this country. This is the same hon. member who, last year, when the reciprocity proposals were before this House, a measure v'hich presented to the people of western Canada at least, a measure of tariff relief, of freer trade and new markets, said that if the reciprocity agreement went through it was one bulwark of the grand old doctrine of protection gone. I am not surprised that he is in favour of a Tariff Commission which is designed to get. excuses to increase the tariff instead of reducing it.
I was more surprised when I heard the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen)who is a friend of mine, and wdiose friendship I hope always to retain, advocating the doctrine of protection in this House this afternoon. I am unable to understand as a western man how' any man in this parliament who represents a western constituency can advocate protection. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) was the gallant champion of the farmers' rights in this country. He was the man who moved

for the reduction of duties on, agricultural implements and at the same time,- when the reciprocity agreement was before the House and the country, an agreement which included the reduction of the duty on agricultural implements, was one of the, most ardent opponents of that agreement. Hon. members must be judged by their actions rather than by their words. I was not so much surprised at the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) to whose addresses I always listen with a great deal- of pleasure, as they are full of poetry, full of eloquence, and whom I am glad to follow in most things except politics. But I apply to him the same remarks as I have applied to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, how any man representing a constituency in western Canada with the economic conditions now existing there can stand here and advocate the doctrine of a high protective tariff, I cannot very well understand, and I think I know something about the economic conditions^ that exist at least in Saskatchewan and in part of the province of Manitoba.
Who advocated a high protective tariff?

My hon. friend has heard what I have to say, I say again that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and the hon. member for Brandon have to-day advocated the maintenance of a protective tariff in Canada.
You said a high protective tariff?

You can take -that out of it if you like, and I have no doubt my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) is prepared to advocate the same views as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. These hon. members during the late parliament and the parliament before, were the most ardent advocates of the reduction of the duties on agricultural implements and yet when the reciprocity proposals came before this House and the country every one of them, when they had a chance of supporting a specific reduction, opposed that particular agreement. That is the position they are in to-day and these gentlemen, ever since I have been in westr ern Canada, have gone through that country stating that the Liberal party had never reduced the tariff and that the Conservative party in western Canada was the party in favour of a low tariff. I have heard these gentlemen say that on the platform. I would support the Liberal policy to-day as during the past few years, if for nothing else than for the reduction of tariff they made in connection with the British preference. That was a substantial reduction in the tariff. The Conservative party has for years been directly opposed as shown by
their speeches and votes in this House, to the British preference. At the ,same time, during the recent election, they shouted loyalty from the housetops and said that we in the west would interfere with the British preference because we wanted to trade more freely with the United States. They say the Liberal party never reduced the tariff and there is no difference in the policies of the parties with respect to the tariff. Every member of this House who is familiar with the records of the Department of Trade and Commerce knows that the average rate of duty on goods dutiable and free entering Canada in 1896 was about 19 per cent, whereas in the past few years under the Liberal administration it has been about 15 per cent. You say that means nothing to the consumers? I say that during the fifteen or sixteen years of the Liberal administration, it saved the people of this country $100,000,000 as compared with what they would have paid if the old Conservative tariff of 1894 had remained in force.
The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) referred to cement this afternoon and he said that the reason for the difference in price of cement in western Canada as compared with Ontario is the excessive freight rates. The hon. member for North Grey was in a measure correct. There is a large difference in the price caused by'the excessive freight rates we pay on cement entering western Canada. But I call attention to this fact that in western Ontario to-day the farmers and the contractors, every consumer, is paying for cement $1.75 per barrel whereas in Buffalo directly across the line, the price is $1.25. What is the cause of that? It is not freight rates, it is that immense cement merger which I believe was one of the greatest steals ever perpetrated in Canada, which has made a millionaire of one man, Max. Aitken, has enabled him to go to the old country, to get a seat in the House of Commons and obtain a knighthood.
And that was all done by the tariff. If these so-called lords of high finance sitting in Montreal can purchase cement plants throughout Canada for twelve million dollars, capitalize them for eighteen million dollars and put the rake-off of six million dollars in their pockets, who is going to pay for all that watered stock. It is the man who buys the cement, the man who wants to put a cement floor in his stable that pays for that over-capitalization. And Sir, I say that is caused by the protective tariff on cement.
But somebody will say to me: what is your position on the tariff; you are a moderate protectionist. Well, I do not acknowledge the name of protectionist at all; I have always supported a tariff for revenue, and I do not believe

in framing a tariff from the standpoint of protection. I believe that the tariff of this country, particularly on the necessaries of life should be reduced. I do not want to see it wiped off altogether, but I say: reduce it gradually. I am not an enemy of the Manufacturers' Association, nor of any manufacturer in this country, but I say there are a great many manufacturing industries in Canada that could reasonably stand a small reduction in the tariff at the present time, and cement is one of them.
Take the tariff on agricultural implements. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) and the Conservative member for the province of Manitoba, will all agree with me when I say that the manufacturers of agricultural implements could reasonably stand a reduction in the tariff to the figure of ten per cent. I do not think that is an unreasonable proposition. I believe that some of my Conservative friends in Manitoba would vote with me in a proposition to reduce the tariff on agricultural implements to ten per cent. These agricultural implement manufacturers have been competing for years with other agricultural implements in Australia and in Eussia, and of recent years in France, and surely they can compete in their own markets with a lower tariff than the present rate of seventeen and a half per cent.
Not long ago I referred to the Canadian tanner's combine in this House, and my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) did not agree with me, and he gave an explanation of why the price of canned goods in western Canada had increased since the formation of the Canadian Can-ners' combine. I may tell the House that during the past year and a half the price of canned goods in my district has increased from fifty per cent to seventy-five per cent on all lines of goods. Is it any wonder that the people of the province of Saskatchewan are not very anxious to support a protectionist tariff for the benefit of the manufacturers?
What is the cause of the increase in the price of canned goods?
My hon friend will not be at a loss to give some explanation for that increased price.
Answer that question if you can.
I will tell you then, it is because the Canadian canners have formed a combine in Ontario and have unduly enhanced the price of canned goods.
That is not so at all.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) has the floor.
Does my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) wish to ask a question?
Yes, you are making a statement which you cannot back up.

I quite realize the anxiety of my hon. friend (Mr Marshall) for whom I have the greatest respect, but I say that the great difficulty with the Tory government we have now in power, is that one half of its supporters in the House are mixed up with combines in the province of Ontario. I do not blame these men for making all they can out of their business, but I am giving you the point of view of the people in the province of Saskatchewan. If I lived in Ontario like my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) I might take a different view of the matter and especially if I held a large block of stock in the Canadian Canners' combine.
I would take the articles which are necessities for the consuming population of this country and I would reduce the tariff on them until it reached, say, a minimum of ten per cent. It may not make much difference to some men in this House who become millionaires by reason of the protective tariff whether they pay five dollars or six dollars for a pair of boots, but it makes a great deal of difference to the people who live in the rural parts of Ontario and Saskatchewan and the other provinces of the Dominion, and so I would reduce the tariff on boots and shoes to a nominal rate. I would take gasolene, and oil, and tinware, and kitchen" utensils and I would reduce the tariff to a minimum on them.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Martin) aware that the late government which he supported raised the duties on boots and shoes by five per cent, and never reduced the tariff on boots and shoes at all?

The hon. gentleman and all other hon. gentlemen who sit on that side of the House are always very anxious to refer to what the late government did. In answer to what my hon. friend has said I want to say that I was not in concurrence with the policy of the late government on matters of tariff and I did not agree with the tariff that was maintained by the late government. I advocated time .and again, although probably not from my place in the House, although I did on two -or three occasions advocate here a reduction in the tariff-but before the various ministers of the government I did advocate the necessity in the interests of western Canada of reducing the tariff

on the necessaries of life. That is the platform I stand on to-day and that is the platform I shall continue to stand on so long as I live in Canada. Will any one tell me what reason th'ere is why by means of a monopoly in tinware, any man in this country should be allowed to become a millionaire by taking money irom the pockets of the common people and putting it into his own pocket? And, Sir, these very same men who control the tin monopoly in Canada when other men wanted to get a tariff of ten per cent put on sheet tin to be manufactured in Canada, came to the late government in a body and opposed any tariff favour being given to anybody but themselves.
Who are they?

My hon. friend knows them and he knows they sit on the government benches and not on this side of the House. I say that in any matter relating to the tariff I shall always view with the greatest suspicion the action of this government because many of the government supporters sitting in this House to-day are interested in the monopolies and trusts and combines in Canada to such an extent that they cannot let the interests of the people of the country appeal to them in connection with such matters when they come before this House.
Order.
Is it not a fact that all these combines which the hon. gentleman speaks of were organized when the Liberal government were in power?

If my hon. friend (Mr. Labor) was sharp enough to get ahead of the Liberal government in organizing a combine he is entitled to great credit for it. I 'have no doubt that my hon. friend (Mr. I. a lor), like the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Marshall), has something to do with the Canadian Can-ners' combine, and I have no doubt that no matter what commodity I refer to some hon. member on that side of the House would get up and put to me a question about it. I want to say that I am in favour of a gradual reduction in duties, especially on the necessaries of life, including such articles as agricultural implements, hoots and shoes, gasolene, oil, cement, canned goods, woollens, and 'all 'articles which may be properly classified as the necessaries of life for the labouring and agricultural population. I believe that no member from the west, whether Liberal or Conservative, will venture to say that this is not a proper policy as f'ar as western Canada is concerned, and so far as the consuming masses in 'any part of Canada are concerned.
Now, there does not seem to be unanimity among the members of the government with respect to the effects of this Bill. The Secretary of State, speaking in Arnprior the other day, said:
The present government would divorce the making of tariffs from political pull; a new departure from the practice of their predecessors. A Bill has been already prepared for the establishing of a Tariff Commission which would thoroughly examine every tariff and see that it was not mixed up with politics.
According to the Secretary of State they are going to take the tariff out of politics, but according to the remarks of the Finance Minister when 'moving the .second reading of this Bill, you cannot take the tariff out of politics and that is not the object of the measure -at all.
Somebody is wrong; I presume it must have been the Secretary of State, because I believe that what the Finance Minister says is perfectly correct, that you cannot take the tariff out of politics, and I do not think we should' try to do so. The tariff is a matter of taxation, and perhaps the most important matter with which this parliament has to deal from year to year. At the same time, there does not seem to be unanimity on this subject even in the ranks of the government themselves.
Now, the only reason given by the government for bringing in this Bill is that it is for the purpose of getting information. We all agree that it is very important that we should have information with respect to goods manufactured in .this country-the cost of the raw material, the cost of labour, the cost of transportation-so as to enable us, when any item of tariff reduction or tariff increase comes before us, to form a proper opinion respecting it. But I say now exactly what I said when I spoke in the debate on the address-that I aim absolutely opposed to any Tariff Commission being appointed in this country which would in any way tend to relieve the government of the day of the responsibility of dealing with the subject of tariff taxation. We can only judge of what is the intention of the government by certain things that have occurred. I would point to one thing that occurred. A request has been made of the Prime Minister to investigate the cement combine; and what does he say? He says: this is a matter for the Tariff Commission. The hon. member for South Wellington yesterday asked the Minister of Customs whether or not certain triphammers would come into this country free of duty. They are not manufactured in Canada, and there is no reason, according to protective principles, why they should not come in free. The Minister of Customs replied that this was a question for the Tariff Commission. Before the Bill

has passed its second reading, the government are actually sheltering themselves from responsibility behind the proposed Tariff Commission.
Why does the government not take steps to investigate the cement combines? Why does it not appoint a committee of this House for that purpose?
Why did not the late government investigate it?
If the late government were in power to-day there would be a committee now to investigate the cement combine.
Wno allowed this combine to be created? Was it not the hon. gentleman's friends who refused to stop it when their attention was called to what was contemplated by the present combine?

My hon. friend talks nonsense. He does not give the com-binesters, the heads of the mergers who sit on his own side of the House the credit of having brains enough to form that cement merger. I have not a personal acquaintance with the men behind the cement combine; no doubt my hon. friend has. I say we can only judge of the object the government have in view in appointing the Tariff Commission by the straws which indicate which way the wind blows. That object is to have a body of men behind which they can shelter themselves from responsibility when any question of tariff increase or tariff reduction is brought before them.
Now, who asked for this commission? Certainly the people whom I represent have never asked for it. The statement has been made in this debate that this matter was discussed from one end of this country to the other. As far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, that is not the case. No Conservative in that province during the recent campaign ever discussed it. We in the west have not asked for it; we would like some time to discuss it; I would like to know what the people of the province of Saskatchewan think of it before I can cast an intelligent vote on this measure. Therefore, I am in favour of delaying this Bill for a time. Some may say, as I have heard Conservative members say in the lobbies of this House, that it does not matter very much what the people of the west think about anything. There is scarcely a man from the province of Ontario sitting in this House to-day who knows anything about the needs of western Canada; otherwise the people of Ontario would not have voted against the reciprocity proposals to enable us to trade more freely with the United States. If I need any proof of what I say, Mr. MARTIN (Regina).
it is found in the fact that just as soon as there is a grain blockade in the west, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Railways asK the Interstate Commerce Commission to reduce the rates on grain to Duluth to correspond with rates to Port Arthur in order to give us temporary relief. Why did they not consider that last September? We have had grain blockades in the west for many years, and shall have them for many years to come, and the only way to give us relief is to allow us to ship our grain over American railways. If hon. gentlemen who occupy prominent positions in the government to-day would go into the province of Saskatchewan and see grain rotting on the farms of men who have not enough money, some of them, to build proper granaries to house their grain, I think they would change their views on this matter.	*
I was rather interested in a declaration of policy by the Minister of Finance. _ I have always regarded the Conservative party as the high protectionist party in this country. There is the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie) for instance, he is a high tariff advocate; so are many other members from the province of Ontario. But I was somewnat interested in what the Minister of Finance said with respect to his policy, and I have no doubt it is the policy of the government with respect to protection. He said:	I am a
believer in adequate protection. He did not define adequate protection.
How do you define high tariff?
I will give my hon. friend a definition of high tarifl given in this House, I think, by the present Senator Taylor, formerly a prominent member of the Conservative party in this House.
A Chinese wall.

They mean a Chinese wall, as the hon. member for Red Deer has just said-a tarifi wall high enough to keep out competition from any foreign country. Either the hon. member for Halton or the hon. member for Peel said he was a believer in putting a Chinese wall around this country so that it would prevent any goods from a foreign country coming into this country at all.
I never heard of it.

I will say for myself that the hon. gentleman has no right to make such a reference to me. I will state what I did say at one time in regard to agricultural protection, that I was prepared to put a Chinese wall around Canada, and for the protection of the western people I am prepared to do it to-day. I spoke of agricultural protection; I made no refer-

ence to manufactured goods. Now I hope the _ hon. gentleman will not repeat that again and misrepresent me.

The hon. gentleman is the last member of the House that I would attempt to misrepresent in anyway; but in reading some of the speeches made by these hon. gentlemen, I got that impression. It may have been somebody else.
If it be necessary for me to deny it, I give the statement the most emphatic denial.

I am somewhat surprised at the anxiety of hon. gentlemen opposite to pose as free traders. We have had a definition of ' adequate protection ' given by hon. gentlemen opposite. According to that definition, it is protection sufficient to keep out the competition of any foreign country. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said that he would be glad to give the people of the west adequate protection to their agricultural products. The people of the west however would not thank him very much for any such protection. What they desire is not protection but more profitable markets for their products and easier access to those markets, but taking the meaning given to adequate protection by the Tory party, namely, protection sufficient to keep out competition from foreign countries, how would that affect the great provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, where there are practically no manufacturing establishments. There is a provision in this Bill which strikes me as somewhat peculiar. We know now that the policy of the government is one of adequate protection. Section 4 provides:
In respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada per the commission shall, under the direction of the minister, make inquiry as
Under a government whose policy is one of adequate protection, the minister, who is the exponent of that policy, is to direct the Tariff Commission to inquire into certain things and report to the minister.
