Mr. Speaker, it is a little difficult to introduce any new information into a debate which has commanded the attention of the House so long as this has done. But I rise, with your permission to speak on the Bill, and to give it my support. I believe that the -principle of the Bill is proper and that the methods by which that principle is to be applied are workable. To my mind, there is no question more important that can engage the attention of parliament than one of this kind, one relating to the tariff which regulates the trade and commerce of our country. The tariff might well be compared to a tree. Trunk, branches, leaves, blossoms and fruit are in Ottawa, but its roots ramify to every part of this great Canada of ours. I think that an unprejudiced survey of the history of Canada since confederation, will convince any unprejudiced inquirer that the people of Canada believe in a protectionist policy. And no hon. member has yet risen in his place who has seen fit to deny that proposition. The hon. member from Regina (Mr. Martin) came near to denying that he was a protectionist, but he himself admitted that he believed in protection for revenue only. The money which we require to carry on our public works, to build our railways, to operate our canals, to dredge our harbours, to light our coasts, to pay our steamship subsidies, to protect our fisheries, and for ali our public services, comes from this source- the tariff. Anything therefore which enters so completely into every phase of our national life is a matter which requires the most serious consideration of *hose whom the Canadian people elect to represent them in parliament.
The Finance Minister has substituted a Bill to create a tariff commission and to define the powers of that commission. Some hon. members have said that behind the clauses of the Bill there lie hidden in the deep recesses of the minds of the Finance Minister and his colleagues a desire to endow that commission with 87i
powers superior to the powers of parliament. Sir, in a democratic country like Canada, that would be impossible. The parliament of Canada could not and would not create a body superior to parliament itself; the creature is always inferior to the creator. And, as I read the Bill, there is no delegation wathever of the powers of parliament. Nor is there any -conflict of power, if I read the Bill correctly, -and I think I do. I anticipate -that the men who are to be appointed on this commission will be, in time at least, specialists in that particular line. Some hon. members who have spoken in opposition to this measure, seem to believe that this commission will have legislative powers. The two gentlemen who spoke first in opposition to this measure, had that in -mind, judging from the tenor of their remarks. This commission can have no legislative powers; at the very most, it can only be an advisory body. Canada is a democratic country, and the men who come here to legislate for Canada and the people of Canada themselves, would not stand for any abrogation of the powers given to parliament.
Parliament is the one body that legislates for the people of Canada, and if the government were to attempt to pass over to a commission that power which parliament possesses, parliament would be exceeding its functions. Now as I construe the meaning of this Bill, this commission is to be purely an advisory body, a body of specialists who shall gather information to submit to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues, upon which they may frame a tariff, should they at any time deem it advisable to do so. The government may accept the advice of this commission, the Bill does not say that they shall accept it; they may not. But that body will be in a position to furnish the Cabinet a large amount of information with respect to the various commodities covered by our tariff, information which they cannot get under the present system. It has been said that the Tariff Commission will not present opinions, but facts. Now if there is anything that the government require in framing a tariff it is facts relating to the cost of production of the various commodities that enter into our complex commercial life. Some one has said that this will result in an irrational tariff. I do not think any argument has been advanced which -supports that -contention. In fact, if I view the Bill aright it will have a tendency to keep a balance a-s between -the manufacturer and the producer in Canada. Now, how is this to be done? It is going to be done by examining the cost of production at home and abroad. The commissioners will have power to investigate conditions, to learn how much it costs to produce the commodities we use in onr everyday life.

It will also have power to take expert advice from specialists in any particular line. It seems to me that information of that kind would be of great use to the Cabinet. The commissioners will be able to find out the cost of the raw material. It has been well said that the raw material of one manufacturer is the finished product of another. I take it that the tariffs of all, countries are more or less approximate to a scientific tariff. I believe it is impossible to frame a real scientific tariff. A tariff can only approximate the actual cost of any commodity. But if this commission submits to our government information that is only approximate as to the cost of an article, it will supply information that no Cabinet of Canada since confederation has ever had. Then they will inquire as to the cost of assembling these raw materials in the final manufacture, and that will include the cost of producing the raw material, and the .transportation to the point of assemblage. After that, it will inquire into the cost of manufacture, and the factors which enter into that are the cost of labour, the cost of the plant and interest thereon, the insurance on the plant, and so forth. Further, they will inquire into the cost of selling that commodity. This is information which has never been given, either to the government or the people of Canada. With this information at hand they will be able to compare the cost of producing these articles in Canada and abroad. Then they will Ibe prepared to advise the government as to what measure of protection is .required upon any one of these commodities.
Mr. Speaker, I am a protectionist, I subscribe to the doctrine of protection. The protection I advocate is the difference between the cost of producing an article by our foreign competitors and the cost of producing that article at home, plus a reasonable profit to our Canadian manufacturer. That is the protection I believe in, and that is the protection which I believe the people of Canada in general endorse. But this profit must not be too large, nor must it be too small. If it is too large, it will create the combines and mergers which some hon. gentlemen opposite referred to. I think this commission, if it lives up to the expectations which we have of it, will prevent absolutely the existence of combines and mergers, that is one of the things which commends it to my mind. The commissioners will have information as to the cost of production which will make it possible for our government to frame a tariff under which combines and mergers cannot profitably exist. I take it that is a field where this commission will find .its most useful work; it will maintain that balance between interests that is so esential for the permanent progress of Canada. Mr. Speaker, any man who studies political economy, even in the most superficial way, will admit that the home market is the best. It is cur desire to preserve this home market. In an agricultural country like this we must have manufacturing communities to consume the products of the soil, the products of the farm, the products of the sea and the products of the mine. That is the policy which we are aiming at, we want to build up a home market which shall consume the products we produce within the borders of our own country. Now the more you reduce the cost of transportation between the producer and the consumer the cheaper will the article be to the consumer. Consequently the home market is the best.

It is, therefore, to build up a home market that the Conservative party has always directed its energies, and I hope always will.
Some one has been good enough to send to the members quotations on the question of trade. I have here a little card sent out by the Canadian Home Market Association. This contains a quotation by one of the greatest presidents the United States ever had, President Lincoln, who said :
I do not know much about the tariff but I know this much:	When we buy goods
abroad we get the goods and the foreigner gets the money. When we buy goods at home we get both the goods and the money.

It is said by some philosophers and people who study political economy that there are three stages in the life of every nation. The first stage is that of free trade in which the nation trades with other nations further advanced in the arts of commerce. The second stage is that in which the nation promotes manufacturing and transportation and adapts commercial regulations and the third stage is that in which that nation gradually reverts to free trade, to lower duties and the removal of the restrictions on trade. If that is true, Canada is in the second stage, we are trying to protect our manufactures, to build up a home market and our history will show that we have mortgaged our future to advance the transportation of our country. Some one has said that this is an innovation. It is no innovation, some of the most advanced nations of the earth are adopting the policy which we are asking the parliament of this country to adopt. My hon. friend opposite yesterday said that this was a cheap Yankee device brought forth from the fertile mind of the Minister of Finance. Are we governed in Canada by the laws of the Medes and Persians that change not? Political economy is a progressive science and Canada, being a progressive country, requires a progressive political economy. We are the heirs of all the ages, we are the people who observe what other nations are doing and adopt anything that commends itself to us. Is that a reason why we should not have one? What are the functions of that board. First to select an article and examine into its sources of supply; (2) to find out the adtual cost of production as near as that may (be, and (3) to

Mr. Speaker, had I spoken earlier in this debate I might have spoken at greater length than 1 intend to-night, but other hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, especially my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) have dealt so exhaustively with the subject and have so ably placed the views of the people I represent before the House that little remains for me to add. However, 1 do not wish to give a silent vote on this important matter and I shall briefly state my views. Last summer the Prime Minister made a trip to the west and he was met at almost every point by delegations of farmers who asked him many questions in connection with the tariff and the reply of the right hon. gentleman always was that he intended if elected to appoint a tariff commission for the purpose of ascertaining the facts. That term ' ascertaining the facts' was a favourite expression of his, and the legislation we have before us to-day is evidently an attempt to carry out that promise on his part. Now, with regard to ascertaining facts I say that we have already ascertained many facts which it does not need the services of a commission to investigate. We have ascertained the fact that agricultural implements are very much dearer than they should be and that the tariff is to a large extent responsible for that. We have also ascertained the fact that the manufacturers of Canada are well able to do without the protection they have been getting. We know that they are able to compete successfully with their rivals in other countries, not only in Great Britain, but in South Africa, Australia, The Argentine, I understand too that even in the United States some Canadian agricultural implements have been sent over there, the duty paid, and actually sold at a less price than the articles manufactured in that country. These facts are known to us and I do not see why there is any necessity for an expensive tariff commission to make inquiry into them. Now, when a western man is speaking about the tariff the question of the duty on agricultural implements generally comes up. Every farmer is anxious to develop his land and he cannot do so unless he has the proper implements which are numerous and expensive, especially in the west. I might mention some of these implements that the farmer requires; he needs a breaking plough, a gang plough, a harrow, a drill, a disc harrow, a reaper, a wagon, etc., and the purchase price of these is a very heavy expense to him. It is not to
the interests of eastern Canada that the farmer should be restricted in his operations and he certainly cannot farm to the same advantage unless he can get the necessary implements at a reasonable price.
I think the very first thing the Tariff Commission should arrange for is that there should be a material reduction on the duties on agricultural implements, but I do not know that we can look for that from any Tariff Commission that will be appointed by a Conservative government.
We heard to-night some of the old protectionist theories that we have been hearing of for many years. We have heard about the benefit of the home market, a market which the people would build up with their own money. After all, we in the west do not find the home market to be a great benefit to us. Take the article of wheat. The quantity of wheat we can consume in Canada is not more than 50,000,000 bushels, and if the production of wheat in Canada were restricted to that quantity, a good many of the manufacturers might close up their businesses; there would not be much smoke coming out of tall chimneys, and there would not be many men employed, to create this home market. The prices of most of the products of the west are based, not upon the prices originating in the home market, but on the export prices. This is true of wheat, cattle and other staple articles. I am not going to belittle the benefit of a home market, but at the same time we may pay too dearly for it, and that is what I think the people are doing. I do not think we can entertain any hope that this Tariff Commission will bring about very much change in that regard.
Now, Sir, I do not say that we should not have a tariff at all. A revenue must be raised, and the farmers like everybody else have to pay their share. It is a question, however, whether or not the implements of industry should not be as nearly free as possible. If the people are encouraged to greater production in that way, the revenue will not suffer. They will have more money with which to buy other duty-paying articles such as luxuries, which I think should bear the greater part of the cost of governing the country. That principle is observed in the tariff with respect to some of the professions, because I find that surgical and dental instruments are on the free list. I am not gioing to object to that. It probably enables surgeons and dentists to procure the most modern instruments, which should of course be encouraged, though 1 do not know that this will have the effect of reducing the fees. I find that there is I no duty on surgical and dental instruments

of metal, surgical needles, X-ray apparatus and parts thereof, surgical operating tables for use in hospitals, and microscopes valued at not less than $50 retail.; also professional and scientific books for the library of any incorporated medical, law, iiterary, scientific or art association or society. These are really the tools of certain professional men. I do not see wily the implements of the farming class should not be dealt with very much on the same line.
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to be much exercised over the manufacturers; they are evidently wedded to their idols. The Tariff Commission is expected to take evidence as to the cost of production, so that the manufacturers can be protected in order that they may make large profits. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not appear to regard it as important to consider the cost of production of what the farmers produce. The cost of agricultural implements enters very_ largely into that, and the farmer is not in the position of the manufacturer in having a fixed price for his product. He has to have more than that-something that he has not now in the west-transportation to the markets. He has to take what he can get and pay the freight charged upon his product. I do not say that these matters can all be controlled, but some things could be controlled. The cost of the implements he has to use could to a certain extent be controlled, and I think the Tariff Commission-which no doubt will be appointed, though we on this side of .the House are qpposed to it-should take that into consideration. In order that there may be some chance of the Tariff Commission doing so, I would suggest that at least one western farmer, or at all events some capable person acquainted with the conditions in the west, be appointed upon it. Then we would have some hope of getting fair-play from this commission. Its usefulness will depend largely upon the personnel ,of its members. In conclusion, I will merely say that I am in favour of the amendment, believing that the government, instead of appointing this commission, should of their own accord bring in a Tariff Bill to reduce the duties very materially, especially on agricultural implements.
